    "# Calculating the root mean square deviation of atomic structures\n",
    "\n",
    "We calculate the RMSD of domains in adenylate kinase as it transitions from an open to closed structure, and look at calculating weighted RMSDs.\n",
    "\n",
    "**Last updated:** December 2022 with MDAnalysis 2.4.0-dev0\n",
    "\n",
    "**Minimum version of MDAnalysis:** 1.0.0\n",
    "\n",
    "**Packages required:**\n",
    "    \n",
    "* MDAnalysis (<a data-cite=\"michaud-agrawal_mdanalysis_2011\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1002/jcc.21787\">Michaud-Agrawal *et al.*, 2011</a>, <a data-cite=\"gowers_mdanalysis_2016\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.25080/Majora-629e541a-00e\">Gowers *et al.*, 2016</a>)\n",
    "* MDAnalysisTests\n",
    "* [pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org)\n",
    "\n",
    "**See also**\n",
    "\n",
    "* [Pairwise (2D) RMSD](pairwise_rmsd.ipynb)\n",
    "* [RMSF](rmsf.ipynb)\n",
    "\n",
    "<div class=\"alert alert-info\">\n",
    "    \n",
    "**Note**\n",
    "\n",
    "MDAnalysis implements RMSD calculation using the fast QCP algorithm (<a data-cite=\"theobald_rapid_2005\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1107/S0108767305015266\">Theobald, 2005</a>). Please cite (<a data-cite=\"theobald_rapid_2005\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1107/S0108767305015266\">Theobald, 2005</a>) when using the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.align`` module in published work.\n",
    "\n",
    "</div>"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 1,
   "metadata": {

   "source": [
    "import MDAnalysis as mda\n",
    "from MDAnalysis.tests.datafiles import PSF, DCD, CRD\n",
    "from MDAnalysis.analysis import rms\n",
    "\n",
    "import pandas as pd\n",
    "# the next line is necessary to display plots in Jupyter\n",
    "%matplotlib inline"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "## Loading files"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "The test files we will be working with here feature adenylate kinase (AdK), a phosophotransferase enzyme. (<a data-cite=\"beckstein_zipping_2009\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmb.2009.09.009\">Beckstein *et al.*, 2009</a>) The trajectory ``DCD`` samples a transition from a closed to an open conformation. AdK has three domains: \n",
    "\n",
    "  * CORE\n",
    "  * LID: an ATP-binding domain\n",
    "  * NMP: an AMP-binding domain\n",
    "  \n",
    "The LID and NMP domains move around the stable CORE as the enzyme transitions between the opened and closed conformations. One way to quantify this movement is by calculating the root mean square deviation (RMSD) of atomic positions."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 2,
   "metadata": {
    "execution": {
     "iopub.execute_input": "2021-05-19T05:56:45.271171Z",
     "iopub.status.busy": "2021-05-19T05:56:45.270526Z",
     "iopub.status.idle": "2021-05-19T05:56:45.612340Z",
     "shell.execute_reply": "2021-05-19T05:56:45.612777Z"
    }
   },
   "outputs": [
    {
     "name": "stderr",
     "output_type": "stream",
     "text": [
      "/home/pbarletta/mambaforge/envs/guide/lib/python3.9/site-packages/MDAnalysis/coordinates/DCD.py:165: DeprecationWarning: DCDReader currently makes independent timesteps by copying self.ts while other readers update self.ts inplace. This behavior will be changed in 3.0 to be the same as other readers. Read more at https://github.com/MDAnalysis/mdanalysis/issues/3889 to learn if this change in behavior might affect you.\n",
      "  warnings.warn(\"DCDReader currently makes independent timesteps\"\n"
     ]
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "u = mda.Universe(PSF, DCD)  # closed AdK (PDB ID: 1AKE)\n",
    "ref = mda.Universe(PSF, CRD)  # open AdK (PDB ID: 4AKE)"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "## Background\n",
    "\n",
    "The root mean square deviation (RMSD) of particle coordinates is one measure of distance, or dissimilarity, between molecular conformations. Each structure should have matching elementwise atoms $i$ in the same order, as the distance between them is calculated and summed for the final result. It is calculated between coordinate arrays $\\mathbf{x}$ and $\\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}$ according to the equation below:\n",
    "\n",
    "$$ \\text{RMSD}(\\mathbf{x}, \\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}) = \\sqrt{\\frac{1}{n} \\sum_{i=1}^{n}{|\\mathbf{x}_i-\\mathbf{x}_i^{\\text{ref}}|^2}} $$\n",
    "\n",
    "As molecules can move around, the structure $\\mathbf{x}$ is usually translated by a vector $\\mathbf{t}$ and rotated by a matrix $\\mathsf{R}$ to align with the reference $\\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}$ such that the RMSD is minimised. The RMSD after this optimal superposition can be expressed as follows:\n",
    "\n",
    "$$ \\text{RMSD}(\\mathbf{x}, \\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}) = \\min_{\\mathsf{R}, \\mathbf{t}} %\n",
    "  \\sqrt{\\frac{1}{N} \\sum_{i=1}^{N} \\left[ %\n",
    "      (\\mathsf{R}\\cdot\\mathbf{x}_{i}(t) + \\mathbf{t}) - \\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\\text{ref}} \\right]^{2}}$$\n",
    "\n",
    "The RMSD between one reference state and a trajectory of structures is often calculated as a way to measure the dissimilarity of the trajectory conformational ensemble to the reference. This reference is frequently the first frame of the trajectory (the default in MDAnalysis), in which case it can provide insight into the overall movement from the initial starting point. While stable RMSD values from a reference structure are frequently used as a measure of conformational convergence, this metric suffers from the problem of *degeneracy*: many different structures can have the same RMSD from the same reference. For an alternative measure, you could use [pairwise or 2D RMSD](pairwise_rmsd.ipynb).\n",
    "\n",
    "Typically not all coordinates in a structures are included in an RMSD analysis. With proteins, the fluctuation of the residue side-chains is not representative of overall conformational change. Therefore when RMSD analyses are performed to investigate large-scale movements in proteins, the atoms are usually restricted only to the backbone atoms (forming the amide-bond chain) or the alpha-carbon atoms. \n",
    "\n",
    "MDAnalysis provides functions and classes to calculate the [RMSD between coordinate arrays](#RMSD-between-two-sets-of-coordinates), and [Universes](#RMSD-of-a-Universe-with-multiple-selections) or [AtomGroups](#RMSD-of-an-AtomGroup-with-multiple-selections). \n",
    "\n",
    "The contribution of each particle $i$ to the final RMSD value can also [be weighted](#Weighted-RMSD-of-a-trajectory) by $w_i$:\n",
    "\n",
    "$$ \\text{RMSD}(\\mathbf{x}, \\mathbf{x}^\\text{ref}) = \\sqrt{\\frac{\\sum_{i=1}^{n}{w_i|\\mathbf{x}_i-\\mathbf{x}_i^{\\text{ref}}|^2}}{\\sum_{i-1}^n w_i}} $$\n",
    "\n",
    "RMSD analyses are frequently weighted by mass. The MDAnalysis RMSD class ([API docs](https://docs.mdanalysis.org/stable/documentation_pages/analysis/rms.html#MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.RMSD)) allows you to both [select mass-weighting](#Mass) with `weights='mass'` or `weights_groupselections='mass'`, or to [pass custom arrays](#Custom-weights) into either keyword."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "## RMSD between two sets of coordinates"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "The ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.rmsd`` function returns the root mean square deviation (in Angstrom) between two sets of coordinates. Here, we calculate the RMSD between the backbone atoms of the open and closed conformations of AdK. Only considering the backbone atoms is often more helpful than calculating the RMSD for all the atoms, as movement in amino acid side-chains isn't indicative of overall conformational change."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 3,
   "metadata": {
    "execution": {
     "iopub.execute_input": "2021-05-19T05:56:45.616996Z",
     "iopub.status.busy": "2021-05-19T05:56:45.616399Z",
     "iopub.status.idle": "2021-05-19T05:56:45.621101Z",
     "shell.execute_reply": "2021-05-19T05:56:45.621515Z"
    }
   },
   "outputs": [
    {
     "data": {
      "text/plain": [
       "6.823686867261616"
      ]
     },
     "execution_count": 3,
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "execute_result"
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "rms.rmsd(u.select_atoms('backbone').positions,  # coordinates to align\n",
    "         ref.select_atoms('backbone').positions,  # reference coordinates\n",
    "         center=True,  # subtract the center of geometry\n",
    "         superposition=True)  # superimpose coordinates"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "## RMSD of a Universe with multiple selections"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {
    "raw_mimetype": "text/restructuredtext"
   },
   "source": [
    "It is more efficient to use the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.RMSD`` class to calculate the RMSD of an entire trajectory to a single reference point, than to use the the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.rmsd`` function.\n",
    "\n",
    "The ``rms.RMSD`` class first performs a rotational and translational alignment of the target trajectory to the reference universe at ``ref_frame``, using the atoms in ``select`` to determine the transformation. The RMSD of the ``select`` selection is calculated. Then, *without further alignment*, the RMSD of each group in ``groupselections`` is calculated. "
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 4,
   "metadata": {
    "execution": {
     "iopub.execute_input": "2021-05-19T05:56:45.624939Z",
     "iopub.status.busy": "2021-05-19T05:56:45.624300Z",
     "iopub.status.idle": "2021-05-19T05:56:45.625772Z",
     "shell.execute_reply": "2021-05-19T05:56:45.626238Z"
    }
   },
   "outputs": [],
   "source": [
    "CORE = 'backbone and (resid 1-29 or resid 60-121 or resid 160-214)'\n",
    "LID = 'backbone and resid 122-159'\n",
    "NMP = 'backbone and resid 30-59'"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 5,
   "metadata": {
    "execution": {
     "iopub.execute_input": "2021-05-19T05:56:45.629913Z",
     "iopub.status.busy": "2021-05-19T05:56:45.629406Z",
     "iopub.status.idle": "2021-05-19T05:56:45.676739Z",
     "shell.execute_reply": "2021-05-19T05:56:45.677176Z"
    }
   },
   "outputs": [
    {
     "data": {
      "text/plain": [
       "<MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.RMSD at 0x7f2e830164f0>"
      ]
     },
     "execution_count": 5,
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "execute_result"
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "R = rms.RMSD(u,  # universe to align\n",
    "             u,  # reference universe or atomgroup\n",
    "             select='backbone',  # group to superimpose and calculate RMSD\n",
    "             groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP],  # groups for RMSD\n",
    "             ref_frame=0)  # frame index of the reference\n",
    "R.run()"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "The data is saved in ``R.rmsd`` as an array."

    "``R.rmsd`` has a row for each timestep. The first two columns of each row are the frame index of the time step, and the time (which is guessed in trajectory formats without timesteps). The third column is RMSD of ``select``. The last few columns are the RMSD of the groups in ``groupselections``."

   "source": [
    "ax = df.plot(x='Frame', y=['Backbone', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'],\n",
    "             kind='line')\n",
    "ax.set_ylabel(r'RMSD ($\\AA$)')"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "## RMSD of an AtomGroup with multiple selections\n",
    "\n",
    "The `RMSD` class accepts both `AtomGroup`s and `Universe`s as arguments. Restricting the atoms considered to an AtomGroup can be very helpful, as the `select` and `groupselections` arguments are applied only to the atoms in the original `AtomGroup`. In the example below, for example, only the alpha-carbons of the CORE domain are incorporated in the analysis.\n",
    "\n",
    "<div class=\"alert alert-info\">\n",
    "    \n",
    "**Note**\n",
    "\n",
    "This feature does not currently support `groupselections`.\n",
    "\n",
    "</div>"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 9,
   "metadata": {
    "execution": {
     "iopub.execute_input": "2021-05-19T05:56:46.106162Z",
     "iopub.status.busy": "2021-05-19T05:56:46.105620Z",
     "iopub.status.idle": "2021-05-19T05:56:46.125735Z",

    }

   "outputs": [
    {
     "data": {
      "text/plain": [
       "<MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.RMSD at 0x7f2e80561610>"
      ]
     },
     "execution_count": 9,
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "execute_result"
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "ca = u.select_atoms('name CA')\n",
    "\n",
    "R = rms.RMSD(ca, ca, select=CORE, ref_frame=0)\n",
    "R.run()"
   ]
  },

   "source": [
    "df = pd.DataFrame(R.results.rmsd, \n",
    "                  columns=['Frame', 'Time (ns)', \n",
    "                           'CORE'])\n",
    "\n",
    "ax = df.plot(x='Frame', y='CORE', kind='line')\n",
    "ax.set_ylabel('RMSD ($\\AA$)')"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "## Weighted RMSD of a trajectory\n",
    "\n",
    "You can also calculate the weighted RMSD of a trajectory using the `weights` and `weights_groupselections` keywords. The former only applies weights to the group in `select`, while the latter must be a list of the *same length and order* as `groupselections`. If you would like to only weight certain groups in `groupselections`, use `None` for the unweighted groups. Both `weights` and `weights_groupselections` accept `None` (for unweighted), `'mass'` (to weight by mass), and custom arrays. A custom array should have the same number of values as there are particles in the corresponding AtomGroup."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "### Mass"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "It is common to weight RMSD analyses by particle weight, so the `RMSD` class accepts `'mass'` as an argument for `weights`. Note that the `weights` keyword only applies to the group in `select`, and does not apply to the `groupselections`; these remain unweighted below."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 11,
   "metadata": {
    "execution": {
     "iopub.execute_input": "2021-05-19T05:56:46.282728Z",
     "iopub.status.busy": "2021-05-19T05:56:46.282209Z",
     "iopub.status.idle": "2021-05-19T05:56:46.334373Z",
     "shell.execute_reply": "2021-05-19T05:56:46.334897Z"
    }
   },
   "outputs": [
    {
     "data": {
      "text/plain": [
       "<MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.RMSD at 0x7f2e804833d0>"
      ]
     },
     "execution_count": 11,
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "execute_result"
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "R_mass = rms.RMSD(u, u,\n",
    "                  select='protein and name CA',\n",
    "                  weights='mass',\n",
    "                  groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP])\n",
    "R_mass.run()"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "The plot looks largely the same as above because all the alpha-carbons and individual backbone atoms have the same mass. Below we show how you can pass in custom weights."
   ]
  },

   "source": [
    "df_mass = pd.DataFrame(R_mass.results.rmsd, \n",
    "                       columns=['Frame', \n",
    "                                'Time (ns)', \n",
    "                                'C-alphas', 'CORE', \n",
    "                                'LID', 'NMP'])\n",
    "ax_mass = df_mass.plot(x='Frame', \n",
    "                       y=['C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'])\n",
    "ax_mass.set_ylabel('Mass-weighted RMSD ($\\AA$)')"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "### Custom weights"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "You can also pass in an array of values for the weights. This must have the same length as the number of atoms in your selection groups. In this example, we pass in arrays of residue numbers. This **is not a typical weighting you might choose**, but we use it here to show how you can get different results to the previous graphs for mass-weighted and non-weighted RMSD. You could choose to pass in an array of charges, or your own custom value. \n",
    "\n",
    "First we select the atom groups to make this easier."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 13,
   "metadata": {
    "execution": {
     "iopub.execute_input": "2021-05-19T05:56:46.507691Z",
     "iopub.status.busy": "2021-05-19T05:56:46.507055Z",
     "iopub.status.idle": "2021-05-19T05:56:46.512950Z",
     "shell.execute_reply": "2021-05-19T05:56:46.513619Z"
    }
   },
   "outputs": [
    {
     "name": "stdout",
     "output_type": "stream",
     "text": [
      "Shape of C-alpha charges: (214,)\n"
     ]
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "ag = u.select_atoms('protein and name CA')\n",
    "print('Shape of C-alpha charges:', ag.charges.shape)\n",
    "core = u.select_atoms(CORE)\n",
    "lid = u.select_atoms(LID)\n",
    "nmp = u.select_atoms(NMP)"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "Below, we pass in weights for `ag` with the `weights` keyword, and weights for the `groupselections` with the `weights_groupselections` keyword."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 14,
   "metadata": {
    "execution": {
     "iopub.execute_input": "2021-05-19T05:56:46.517921Z",
     "iopub.status.busy": "2021-05-19T05:56:46.517384Z",
     "iopub.status.idle": "2021-05-19T05:56:46.565239Z",
     "shell.execute_reply": "2021-05-19T05:56:46.565638Z"
    }
   },
   "outputs": [
    {
     "data": {
      "text/plain": [
       "<MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.RMSD at 0x7f2e80483490>"
      ]
     },
     "execution_count": 14,
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "execute_result"
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "R_charge = rms.RMSD(u, u,\n",
    "                    select='protein and name CA',\n",
    "                    groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP],\n",
    "                    weights=ag.resids,\n",
    "                    weights_groupselections=[core.resids, \n",
    "                                             lid.resids, \n",
    "                                             nmp.resids])\n",
    "R_charge.run()"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "You can see in the below graph that the NMP domain has much higher RMSD than before, as each particle is weighted by its residue number. Conversely, the CORE domain doesn't really change much. We could potentially infer from this that residues later in the NMP domain (with a higher residue number) are mobile during the length of the trajectory, whereas residues later in the CORE domain do not seem to contribute significantly to the RMSD.\n",
    "\n",
    "However, again, this is a **very non-conventional metric** and is shown here simply to demonstrate how to use the code."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 15,
   "metadata": {

    }

   "source": [
    "df_charge = pd.DataFrame(R_charge.results.rmsd, \n",
    "                         columns=['Frame', \n",
    "                                'Time (ns)', \n",
    "                                'C-alphas', 'CORE', \n",
    "                                'LID', 'NMP'])\n",
    "ax_charge = df_charge.plot(x='Frame',\n",
    "                           y=['C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'])\n",
    "ax_charge.set_ylabel('Charge-weighted RMSD ($\\AA$)')"
   ]
  },

   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "## References\n",

# # Calculating the root mean square deviation of atomic structures
#
# We calculate the RMSD of domains in adenylate kinase as it transitions from an open to closed structure, and look at calculating weighted RMSDs.
#
# **Last updated:** December 2022 with MDAnalysis 2.4.0-dev0
#
# **Minimum version of MDAnalysis:** 1.0.0
#
# **Packages required:**
#     
# * MDAnalysis (<a data-cite="michaud-agrawal_mdanalysis_2011" href="https://doi.org/10.1002/jcc.21787">Michaud-Agrawal *et al.*, 2011</a>, <a data-cite="gowers_mdanalysis_2016" href="https://doi.org/10.25080/Majora-629e541a-00e">Gowers *et al.*, 2016</a>)
# * MDAnalysisTests
# * [pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org)
#
# **See also**
#
# * [Pairwise (2D) RMSD](pairwise_rmsd.ipynb)
# * [RMSF](rmsf.ipynb)
#
# <div class="alert alert-info">
#     
# **Note**
#
# MDAnalysis implements RMSD calculation using the fast QCP algorithm (<a data-cite="theobald_rapid_2005" href="https://doi.org/10.1107/S0108767305015266">Theobald, 2005</a>). Please cite (<a data-cite="theobald_rapid_2005" href="https://doi.org/10.1107/S0108767305015266">Theobald, 2005</a>) when using the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.align`` module in published work.
#
# </div>

import MDAnalysis as mda
from MDAnalysis.tests.datafiles import PSF, DCD, CRD
from MDAnalysis.analysis import rms

import pandas as pd
# the next line is necessary to display plots in Jupyter
# Notebook presentation directive: %matplotlib inline


# ## Loading files

# The test files we will be working with here feature adenylate kinase (AdK), a phosophotransferase enzyme. (<a data-cite="beckstein_zipping_2009" href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmb.2009.09.009">Beckstein *et al.*, 2009</a>) The trajectory ``DCD`` samples a transition from a closed to an open conformation. AdK has three domains: 
#
#   * CORE
#   * LID: an ATP-binding domain
#   * NMP: an AMP-binding domain
#   
# The LID and NMP domains move around the stable CORE as the enzyme transitions between the opened and closed conformations. One way to quantify this movement is by calculating the root mean square deviation (RMSD) of atomic positions.

u = mda.Universe(PSF, DCD)  # closed AdK (PDB ID: 1AKE)
ref = mda.Universe(PSF, CRD)  # open AdK (PDB ID: 4AKE)

# ## Background
#
# The root mean square deviation (RMSD) of particle coordinates is one measure of distance, or dissimilarity, between molecular conformations. Each structure should have matching elementwise atoms $i$ in the same order, as the distance between them is calculated and summed for the final result. It is calculated between coordinate arrays $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{x}^{\text{ref}}$ according to the equation below:
#
# $$ \text{RMSD}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{\text{ref}}) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n}{|\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}_i^{\text{ref}}|^2}} $$
#
# As molecules can move around, the structure $\mathbf{x}$ is usually translated by a vector $\mathbf{t}$ and rotated by a matrix $\mathsf{R}$ to align with the reference $\mathbf{x}^{\text{ref}}$ such that the RMSD is minimised. The RMSD after this optimal superposition can be expressed as follows:
#
# $$ \text{RMSD}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{\text{ref}}) = \min_{\mathsf{R}, \mathbf{t}} %
#   \sqrt{\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left[ %
#       (\mathsf{R}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{i}(t) + \mathbf{t}) - \mathbf{x}_{i}^{\text{ref}} \right]^{2}}$$
#
# The RMSD between one reference state and a trajectory of structures is often calculated as a way to measure the dissimilarity of the trajectory conformational ensemble to the reference. This reference is frequently the first frame of the trajectory (the default in MDAnalysis), in which case it can provide insight into the overall movement from the initial starting point. While stable RMSD values from a reference structure are frequently used as a measure of conformational convergence, this metric suffers from the problem of *degeneracy*: many different structures can have the same RMSD from the same reference. For an alternative measure, you could use [pairwise or 2D RMSD](pairwise_rmsd.ipynb).
#
# Typically not all coordinates in a structures are included in an RMSD analysis. With proteins, the fluctuation of the residue side-chains is not representative of overall conformational change. Therefore when RMSD analyses are performed to investigate large-scale movements in proteins, the atoms are usually restricted only to the backbone atoms (forming the amide-bond chain) or the alpha-carbon atoms. 
#
# MDAnalysis provides functions and classes to calculate the [RMSD between coordinate arrays](#RMSD-between-two-sets-of-coordinates), and [Universes](#RMSD-of-a-Universe-with-multiple-selections) or [AtomGroups](#RMSD-of-an-AtomGroup-with-multiple-selections). 
#
# The contribution of each particle $i$ to the final RMSD value can also [be weighted](#Weighted-RMSD-of-a-trajectory) by $w_i$:
#
# $$ \text{RMSD}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^\text{ref}) = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}{w_i|\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}_i^{\text{ref}}|^2}}{\sum_{i-1}^n w_i}} $$
#
# RMSD analyses are frequently weighted by mass. The MDAnalysis RMSD class ([API docs](https://docs.mdanalysis.org/stable/documentation_pages/analysis/rms.html#MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.RMSD)) allows you to both [select mass-weighting](#Mass) with `weights='mass'` or `weights_groupselections='mass'`, or to [pass custom arrays](#Custom-weights) into either keyword.

# ## RMSD between two sets of coordinates

# The ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.rmsd`` function returns the root mean square deviation (in Angstrom) between two sets of coordinates. Here, we calculate the RMSD between the backbone atoms of the open and closed conformations of AdK. Only considering the backbone atoms is often more helpful than calculating the RMSD for all the atoms, as movement in amino acid side-chains isn't indicative of overall conformational change.

rms.rmsd(u.select_atoms('backbone').positions,  # coordinates to align
         ref.select_atoms('backbone').positions,  # reference coordinates
         center=True,  # subtract the center of geometry
         superposition=True)  # superimpose coordinates

# ## RMSD of a Universe with multiple selections

# It is more efficient to use the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.RMSD`` class to calculate the RMSD of an entire trajectory to a single reference point, than to use the the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.rmsd`` function.
#
# The ``rms.RMSD`` class first performs a rotational and translational alignment of the target trajectory to the reference universe at ``ref_frame``, using the atoms in ``select`` to determine the transformation. The RMSD of the ``select`` selection is calculated. Then, *without further alignment*, the RMSD of each group in ``groupselections`` is calculated. 

CORE = 'backbone and (resid 1-29 or resid 60-121 or resid 160-214)'
LID = 'backbone and resid 122-159'
NMP = 'backbone and resid 30-59'

R = rms.RMSD(u,  # universe to align
             u,  # reference universe or atomgroup
             select='backbone',  # group to superimpose and calculate RMSD
             groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP],  # groups for RMSD
             ref_frame=0)  # frame index of the reference
R.run()

# The data is saved in ``R.rmsd`` as an array.

R.results.rmsd.shape

# ``R.rmsd`` has a row for each timestep. The first two columns of each row are the frame index of the time step, and the time (which is guessed in trajectory formats without timesteps). The third column is RMSD of ``select``. The last few columns are the RMSD of the groups in ``groupselections``.

# ### Plotting the data
#
# We can easily plot this data using the common data analysis package [pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org). We turn the ``R.rmsd`` array into a [DataFrame](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/dsintro.html#dataframe) and label each column below.

df = pd.DataFrame(R.results.rmsd, 
                  columns=['Frame', 'Time (ns)', 
                           'Backbone', 'CORE', 
                           'LID', 'NMP'])

df

ax = df.plot(x='Frame', y=['Backbone', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'],
             kind='line')
ax.set_ylabel(r'RMSD ($\AA$)')

# ## RMSD of an AtomGroup with multiple selections
#
# The `RMSD` class accepts both `AtomGroup`s and `Universe`s as arguments. Restricting the atoms considered to an AtomGroup can be very helpful, as the `select` and `groupselections` arguments are applied only to the atoms in the original `AtomGroup`. In the example below, for example, only the alpha-carbons of the CORE domain are incorporated in the analysis.
#
# <div class="alert alert-info">
#     
# **Note**
#
# This feature does not currently support `groupselections`.
#
# </div>

ca = u.select_atoms('name CA')

R = rms.RMSD(ca, ca, select=CORE, ref_frame=0)
R.run()

df = pd.DataFrame(R.results.rmsd, 
                  columns=['Frame', 'Time (ns)', 
                           'CORE'])

ax = df.plot(x='Frame', y='CORE', kind='line')
ax.set_ylabel('RMSD ($\AA$)')

# ## Weighted RMSD of a trajectory
#
# You can also calculate the weighted RMSD of a trajectory using the `weights` and `weights_groupselections` keywords. The former only applies weights to the group in `select`, while the latter must be a list of the *same length and order* as `groupselections`. If you would like to only weight certain groups in `groupselections`, use `None` for the unweighted groups. Both `weights` and `weights_groupselections` accept `None` (for unweighted), `'mass'` (to weight by mass), and custom arrays. A custom array should have the same number of values as there are particles in the corresponding AtomGroup.

# ### Mass

# It is common to weight RMSD analyses by particle weight, so the `RMSD` class accepts `'mass'` as an argument for `weights`. Note that the `weights` keyword only applies to the group in `select`, and does not apply to the `groupselections`; these remain unweighted below.

R_mass = rms.RMSD(u, u,
                  select='protein and name CA',
                  weights='mass',
                  groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP])
R_mass.run()

# The plot looks largely the same as above because all the alpha-carbons and individual backbone atoms have the same mass. Below we show how you can pass in custom weights.

df_mass = pd.DataFrame(R_mass.results.rmsd, 
                       columns=['Frame', 
                                'Time (ns)', 
                                'C-alphas', 'CORE', 
                                'LID', 'NMP'])
ax_mass = df_mass.plot(x='Frame', 
                       y=['C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'])
ax_mass.set_ylabel('Mass-weighted RMSD ($\AA$)')

# ### Custom weights

# You can also pass in an array of values for the weights. This must have the same length as the number of atoms in your selection groups. In this example, we pass in arrays of residue numbers. This **is not a typical weighting you might choose**, but we use it here to show how you can get different results to the previous graphs for mass-weighted and non-weighted RMSD. You could choose to pass in an array of charges, or your own custom value. 
#
# First we select the atom groups to make this easier.

ag = u.select_atoms('protein and name CA')
print('Shape of C-alpha charges:', ag.charges.shape)
core = u.select_atoms(CORE)
lid = u.select_atoms(LID)
nmp = u.select_atoms(NMP)

# Below, we pass in weights for `ag` with the `weights` keyword, and weights for the `groupselections` with the `weights_groupselections` keyword.

R_charge = rms.RMSD(u, u,
                    select='protein and name CA',
                    groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP],
                    weights=ag.resids,
                    weights_groupselections=[core.resids, 
                                             lid.resids, 
                                             nmp.resids])
R_charge.run()

# You can see in the below graph that the NMP domain has much higher RMSD than before, as each particle is weighted by its residue number. Conversely, the CORE domain doesn't really change much. We could potentially infer from this that residues later in the NMP domain (with a higher residue number) are mobile during the length of the trajectory, whereas residues later in the CORE domain do not seem to contribute significantly to the RMSD.
#
# However, again, this is a **very non-conventional metric** and is shown here simply to demonstrate how to use the code.

df_charge = pd.DataFrame(R_charge.results.rmsd, 
                         columns=['Frame', 
                                'Time (ns)', 
                                'C-alphas', 'CORE', 
                                'LID', 'NMP'])
ax_charge = df_charge.plot(x='Frame',
                           y=['C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'])
ax_charge.set_ylabel('Charge-weighted RMSD ($\AA$)')

Cell 6 · markdown

Background

The root mean square deviation (RMSD) of particle coordinates is one measure of distance, or dissimilarity, between molecular conformations. Each structure should have matching elementwise atoms $i$ in the same order, as the distance between them is calculated and summed for the final result. It is calculated between coordinate arrays $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{x}^{\text{ref}}$ according to the equation below:

$$ \text{RMSD}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{\text{ref}}) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n}{|\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}_i^{\text{ref}}|^2}} $$

As molecules can move around, the structure $\mathbf{x}$ is usually translated by a vector $\mathbf{t}$ and rotated by a matrix $\mathsf{R}$ to align with the reference $\mathbf{x}^{\text{ref}}$ such that the RMSD is minimised. The RMSD after this optimal superposition can be expressed as follows:

$$ \text{RMSD}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{\text{ref}}) = \min_{\mathsf{R}, \mathbf{t}} % \sqrt{\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left[ % (\mathsf{R}\cdot\mathbf{x}{i}(t) + \mathbf{t}) - \mathbf{x}{i}^{\text{ref}} \right]^{2}}$$

The RMSD between one reference state and a trajectory of structures is often calculated as a way to measure the dissimilarity of the trajectory conformational ensemble to the reference. This reference is frequently the first frame of the trajectory (the default in MDAnalysis), in which case it can provide insight into the overall movement from the initial starting point. While stable RMSD values from a reference structure are frequently used as a measure of conformational convergence, this metric suffers from the problem of degeneracy: many different structures can have the same RMSD from the same reference. For an alternative measure, you could use pairwise or 2D RMSD.

Typically not all coordinates in a structures are included in an RMSD analysis. With proteins, the fluctuation of the residue side-chains is not representative of overall conformational change. Therefore when RMSD analyses are performed to investigate large-scale movements in proteins, the atoms are usually restricted only to the backbone atoms (forming the amide-bond chain) or the alpha-carbon atoms.

MDAnalysis provides functions and classes to calculate the RMSD between coordinate arrays, and Universes or AtomGroups.

The contribution of each particle $i$ to the final RMSD value can also be weighted by $w_i$:

$$ \text{RMSD}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^\text{ref}) = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}{w_i|\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}i^{\text{ref}}|^2}}{\sum{i-1}^n w_i}} $$

RMSD analyses are frequently weighted by mass. The MDAnalysis RMSD class (API docs) allows you to both select mass-weighting with weights='mass' or weights_groupselections='mass', or to pass custom arrays into either keyword.

Cell 7 · markdown

RMSD between two sets of coordinates

Cell 8 · markdown

The MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.rmsd function returns the root mean square deviation (in Angstrom) between two sets of coordinates. Here, we calculate the RMSD between the backbone atoms of the open and closed conformations of AdK. Only considering the backbone atoms is often more helpful than calculating the RMSD for all the atoms, as movement in amino acid side-chains isn't indicative of overall conformational change.

The rms.RMSD class first performs a rotational and translational alignment of the target trajectory to the reference universe at ref_frame, using the atoms in select to determine the transformation. The RMSD of the select selection is calculated. Then, without further alignment, the RMSD of each group in groupselections is calculated.

A custom array should have the same number of values as there are particles in the corresponding AtomGroup.

ax_mass.set_ylabel('Mass-weighted RMSD ($\AA$)')
Cell 29 · markdown

Custom weights

Cell 30 · markdown

You can also pass in an array of values for the weights. This must have the same length as the number of atoms in your selection groups. In this example, we pass in arrays of residue numbers. This is not a typical weighting you might choose, but we use it here to show how you can get different results to the previous graphs for mass-weighted and non-weighted RMSD. You could choose to pass in an array of charges, or your own custom value.

First we select the atom groups to make this easier.

Cell 31 · code
ag = u.select_atoms('protein and name CA')
print('Shape of C-alpha charges:', ag.charges.shape)
core = u.select_atoms(CORE)
lid = u.select_atoms(LID)
nmp = u.select_atoms(NMP)
Cell 32 · markdown

Below, we pass in weights for ag with the weights keyword, and weights for the groupselections with the weights_groupselections keyword.

Cell 33 · code
R_charge = rms.RMSD(u, u,
                    select='protein and name CA',
                    groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP],
                    weights=ag.resids,
                    weights_groupselections=[core.resids, 
                                             lid.resids, 
                                             nmp.resids])
R_charge.run()
Cell 34 · markdown

You can see in the below graph that the NMP domain has much higher RMSD than before, as each particle is weighted by its residue number. Conversely, the CORE domain doesn't really change much. We could potentially infer from this that residues later in the NMP domain (with a higher residue number) are mobile during the length of the trajectory, whereas residues later in the CORE domain do not seem to contribute significantly to the RMSD.

However, again, this is a very non-conventional metric and is shown here simply to demonstrate how to use the code.

Cell 35 · code
df_charge = pd.DataFrame(R_charge.results.rmsd, 
                         columns=['Frame', 
                                'Time (ns)', 
                                'C-alphas', 'CORE', 
                                'LID', 'NMP'])
ax_charge = df_charge.plot(x='Frame',
                           y=['C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'])
ax_charge.set_ylabel('Charge-weighted RMSD ($\AA$)')

Quantify the open–closed transition in five RMSD analyses

The published solver question is below. Reference answers and grading code are separate from solver inputs.

Solver question

autonomous-runs/053/explorer-evidence/native/tasks/autonomous-rmsd-053/instruction.md

Task: RMSD analysis of the adenylate kinase open↔closed transition

Adenylate kinase (AdK) has a stable CORE domain flanked by the LID and NMP domains, which move as the enzyme transitions between closed and open conformations. You are supplied with the topology, a trajectory sampling the closed→open transition, and the open-conformation coordinates. Quantify this conformational change by computing the root mean square deviation (RMSD) of atomic positions, in Angstrom, in five analyses below.

Supplied inputs

  • inputs/adk.psf — protein topology (PSF) for the AdK structure; 214 residues with atom counts and atom order shared by all supplied coordinate data.
  • inputs/adk_trajectory.dcd — trajectory (DCD) sampling the closed→open transition.
  • inputs/adk_open.crd — coordinates (CRD) of the open conformation of the same structure.

Definitions

For coordinate arrays x (one row per atom, atoms in matching order between compared structures) and reference x^(ref):

  • RMSD(x, x^(ref)) = sqrt( (1/n) Σᵢ |xᵢ − xᵢ^(ref)|² )
  • Weighted RMSD(x, x^(ref)) = sqrt( Σᵢ wᵢ |xᵢ − xᵢ^(ref)|² / Σᵢ wᵢ ) (invariant to any overall positive scaling of the weights).
  • Optimal superposition: the displacement / rotation pair that minimizes the (weighted) RMSD; rotations are proper (determinant +1). RMSD under optimal superposition is the minimum over such pairs, with coordinates first expressed relative to the appropriate weighted centroid.
  • Backbone atoms: the main-chain protein atoms (N, CA, C, O).
  • Domains (residue numbers as in the topology):
    • CORE = backbone atoms of residues 1–29, 60–121, 160–214
    • LID = backbone atoms of residues 122–159
    • NMP = backbone atoms of residues 30–59

Required analyses

A. Open vs. closed endpoint conformations. RMSD between the backbone atoms of the open structure (adk_open.crd) and the trajectory's first frame (closed conformation). Subtract the center of geometry of each set, apply optimal superposition, and report the resulting backbone RMSD.

B–E. Trajectory RMSD versus frame 0. For each of the analyses below, the reference is frame 0 of the trajectory itself. For each trajectory frame, first superimpose the frame onto frame 0 by the optimal (weighted, where weights are specified) rigid-body transformation determined by the fitting group; then report:

  1. the RMSD of the fitting group under that fit; and
  2. for each listed domain group, the RMSD between the frame's transformed coordinates and the untransformed frame-0 coordinates of that group's atoms, computed without any further fitting, centering, or re-alignment of the group (the group RMSD measures residual domain displacement under the single global superposition).

B. Backbone and domains (unweighted). Fitting group: all backbone atoms, unweighted. Report four series: backbone (under the fit), CORE, LID, NMP (group RMSDs, unweighted). Group atom sets are the backbone atoms of the full structure given by the domain definitions above.

C. CORE restricted to alpha-carbons. Restrict the entire analysis to the alpha-carbon (CA) atoms. Fitting group: the alpha-carbons of the CORE domain. Report the CORE fit RMSD.

D. Mass-weighted. Fitting group: all alpha-carbons of the protein, with each atom weighted by its mass (mass-weighted centroids for the superposition). Report the mass-weighted fit RMSD for the alpha-carbons, and mass-weighted group RMSDs for CORE, LID, NMP. Group atom sets are the backbone atoms of the full structure (not restricted to alpha-carbons), and the group RMSDs are also mass-weighted (each atom weighted by its mass).

E. Residue-number-weighted. Same structure as D, but each atom is weighted by its residue number instead of its mass — in the fitting group (alpha-carbons of the protein) and in the CORE, LID, NMP group RMSDs (backbone atoms, full structure, weighted by residue number).

Note that in D and E the fitting group and the reported group RMSDs use the specified weighting; the groups being compared are the full-structure backbone atom sets, independent of the alpha-carbon restriction on the fitting group.

Required outputs

Write CSV files (UTF-8, one header row, comma-separated) under outputs/. All RMSD values are in Angstrom and must be finite. Each trajectory table contains exactly one row per trajectory frame, ordered by strictly increasing frame index (the row order is the time series). The frame column is the 0-based trajectory frame index. Do not output a time column.

  1. outputs/rmsd_backbone_open_closed.csv — analysis A. Columns: rmsd_backbone_angstrom. One data row.
  2. outputs/rmsd_backbone_domains.csv — analysis B. Columns: frame, rmsd_backbone_angstrom, rmsd_core_angstrom, rmsd_lid_angstrom, rmsd_nmp_angstrom.
  3. outputs/rmsd_ca_core.csv — analysis C. Columns: frame, rmsd_core_ca_angstrom.
  4. outputs/rmsd_mass_weighted.csv — analysis D. Columns: frame, rmsd_ca_mass_angstrom, rmsd_core_mass_angstrom, rmsd_lid_mass_angstrom, rmsd_nmp_mass_angstrom.
  5. outputs/rmsd_resid_weighted.csv — analysis E. Columns: frame, rmsd_ca_resid_angstrom, rmsd_core_resid_angstrom, rmsd_lid_resid_angstrom, rmsd_nmp_resid_angstrom.

The frame identity is shared across outputs 2–5: each must cover exactly the same set of trajectory frames, once each, in the same order. The RMSD at frame 0 is expected to be near zero (floating-point rounding of identical conformations), not exactly zero.

Environment and limits

CPU-only; no network access; run within 600 seconds and 8 GiB RAM. Software choice is open: any tools may be used as long as the outputs above are produced. For convenience, a compatible offline environment (MDAnalysis 2.11.0, NumPy, pandas) can be supplied; using it is not a requirement.

Acceptance rules

Grading rules (acceptance addendum)

The task question above defines the science. This addendum fixes exactly how submissions are compared. All RMSD quantities are in Angstrom. Software choice is open: any implementation that produces the declared values is acceptable.

1. Declared outputs and paths

Exactly five files are graded, each read at <name> relative to the output root supplied to the grader (in the solution environment this root is /workspace/outputs):

  1. rmsd_backbone_open_closed.csv — analysis A
  2. rmsd_backbone_domains.csv — analysis B
  3. rmsd_ca_core.csv — analysis C
  4. rmsd_mass_weighted.csv — analysis D
  5. rmsd_resid_weighted.csv — analysis E

A file present only under an additional directory layer below the output root (e.g. a further outputs/ subdirectory) is not at its declared path and counts as missing. Undeclared extra files are ignored.

2. CSV structure (each file)

  • UTF-8 text, comma-separated values, exactly one header row followed by data rows. LF or CRLF line endings are both accepted.
  • The header must be exactly the published column list for that file — same names, same order; no missing, extra, renamed or reordered columns (in particular, no time column).
  • Every data row must contain exactly one field per header column. Blank, ragged or padded rows fail. A file with no data row fails.
  • Every field (in all columns, including frame) must parse as a single finite decimal number: optional sign, optional decimal point, optional exponent notation. Empty fields and NaN/Inf (any case) fail. A cell of the exact form np.float64(<finite number>) is also accepted and read as the enclosed number. RMSD values must be nonnegative; frame values must be integers.
  • rmsd_backbone_open_closed.csv must contain exactly one data row.
  • Each of outputs 2–5 must contain exactly one data row per trajectory frame: the frame column holds the complete 0-based index series 0, 1, …, F−1, each frame exactly once, in strictly increasing order, so that row k carries frame k. Missing, duplicated, out-of-order or non-contiguous frames fail. The required row count F is the number of frames of the supplied trajectory and is taken from the reference tables, not from the submission.
  • Outputs 2–5 must present the same frame series (identical set, identical order, identical count); this cross-table frame identity is checked separately.

3. Numeric comparison

Each submission value is compared to the reference value of the same file, the same column and the same frame index (for output 1, its single value), one-to-one by row. Coverage, order and multiplicity all matter: rows are never compared as a set, and a table that drops, adds, duplicates or reorders rows fails. With submission value v and reference value r:

PASS  if and only if  |v − r| ≤ 1×10⁻⁵ + 1×10⁻⁹ × |r|

The relative term uses the reference value as its denominator. The bound is inclusive and must hold for every value cell of the file.

Tolerance basis: the reference tables are computed in double precision from the supplied inputs. At frame 0 the reference itself carries only the floating-point self-RMSD rounding of identical conformations (below about 1×10⁻⁶ Å in every recorded reference table; the task question itself states the frame-0 RMSD is near-zero rounding, not exactly zero), so a submission reporting exactly 0 — or its own equivalent rounding noise — at frame 0 passes through the absolute term. The absolute term 1×10⁻⁵ Å is at least an order of magnitude above that rounding scale; it also covers faithful double-precision recomputation as demonstrated by controls: an independently implemented weighted-Kabsch optimal-superposition recomputation passed every value comparison within this bound (its author additionally reports, but the executed controls alone do not establish, far closer spot-check agreement), and decimal text rounding is bounded by 5×10⁻⁶ Å at 5 decimal places, which still passes, while about 4 or fewer decimals can fail for values near these tables' upper range (several Å). Executed wrong submissions demonstrate the bound's low end of rejection: a deliberately off-tolerance 2×10⁻⁵ Å perturbation and the executed wrong-method variants, with deviations from roughly 1×10⁻³ Å up to several Å, all fail with clear margin. The bound is a limit on observable output differences, not a guarantee that every wrong method is detected in every cell: a value wrong by less than 1×10⁻⁵ Å + 1×10⁻⁹|r| in a given cell passes by construction, and different weighting schemes can agree to about 1×10⁻⁷ Å at frame 0. Textual formatting (digit count, exponent style, trailing zeros, quoted or plain number text) is free as long as the parsed values satisfy the rule.

Each file is graded independently; any single failing value, row or structural defect fails that file's check, and overall acceptance is the conjunction of all checks.

Task directories

Read the supplied inputs from /workspace/inputs/. Write all required output files under /workspace/outputs/, using the relative filenames specified above. The working directory is /workspace. Aliases /inputs/ and /outputs/ refer to these same directories.

Deterministic grader

autonomous-runs/053/explorer-evidence/grading/grade.py

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Deterministic scientific grader for the adenylate-kinase RMSD task.

Reads the five declared CSV outputs from the reference and submission
directories, validates their structure, and compares the parsed scientific
content (frame series and RMSD values in Angstrom) against the reference.

Usage:
    python grade.py --reference-dir PATH --submission-dir PATH --report PATH

The report JSON has exactly the keys {"passed", "checks"}; each check has the
keys {"id", "passed", "message"}. Every declared check is emitted exactly once,
also for missing, malformed or empty submissions. The grader never modifies
reference or submission files and never imports submission code.
"""

import argparse
import csv
import json
import math
import os
import re

SINGLE_OUTPUT = ("rmsd_backbone_open_closed.csv",
                 ("rmsd_backbone_angstrom",))

TRAJECTORY_OUTPUTS = [
    ("rmsd_backbone_domains.csv",
     ("frame", "rmsd_backbone_angstrom", "rmsd_core_angstrom",
      "rmsd_lid_angstrom", "rmsd_nmp_angstrom")),
    ("rmsd_ca_core.csv",
     ("frame", "rmsd_core_ca_angstrom")),
    ("rmsd_mass_weighted.csv",
     ("frame", "rmsd_ca_mass_angstrom", "rmsd_core_mass_angstrom",
      "rmsd_lid_mass_angstrom", "rmsd_nmp_mass_angstrom")),
    ("rmsd_resid_weighted.csv",
     ("frame", "rmsd_ca_resid_angstrom", "rmsd_core_resid_angstrom",
      "rmsd_lid_resid_angstrom", "rmsd_nmp_resid_angstrom")),
]

# Numeric acceptance rule: PASS iff |v - r| <= TOL_ABS + TOL_REL * |r|,
# with r the reference value (inclusive bound).
TOL_ABS = 1e-5   # Angstrom
TOL_REL = 1e-9

_NUMPY_FLOAT64_REPR = re.compile(r"^np\.float64\((.*)\)$", re.DOTALL)


class TableError(Exception):
    """Missing, malformed or invalid CSV output."""


def parse_number(cell):
    """Return the finite float denoted by a CSV cell, or None."""
    if cell is None:
        return None
    text = cell.strip()
    if not text:
        return None
    match = _NUMPY_FLOAT64_REPR.match(text)
    if match:
        text = match.group(1).strip()
        if not text:
            return None
    try:
        value = float(text)
    except (ValueError, OverflowError):
        return None
    if not math.isfinite(value):
        return None
    return value


def allowance(reference):
    """Maximum accepted |v - reference| for a reference value."""
    return TOL_ABS + TOL_REL * abs(reference)


def read_csv_table(directory, filename):
    path = os.path.join(directory, filename)
    if not os.path.isfile(path):
        raise TableError("%s: file not found under the supplied output root"
                         % filename)
    try:
        with open(path, "r", newline="", encoding="utf-8-sig") as handle:
            table = [row for row in csv.reader(handle)]
    except (OSError, UnicodeDecodeError, csv.Error) as exc:
        raise TableError("%s: cannot be read as CSV (%s)" % (filename, exc))
    if not table:
        raise TableError("%s: file has no header row" % filename)
    return table[0], table[1:]


def load_single_output(directory):
    """Load and validate the single-value endpoint (analysis A)."""
    filename, columns = SINGLE_OUTPUT
    header, rows = read_csv_table(directory, filename)
    if list(header) != list(columns):
        raise TableError("%s: header must be exactly %s"
                         % (filename, list(columns)))
    if len(rows) != 1:
        raise TableError("%s: expected exactly 1 data row, found %d"
                         % (filename, len(rows)))
    row = rows[0]
    if len(row) != len(columns):
        raise TableError("%s: data row has %d fields, expected %d"
                         % (filename, len(row), len(columns)))
    value = parse_number(row[0])
    if value is None:
        raise TableError("%s: value %r does not parse as a finite number"
                         % (filename, row[0]))
    return value


def load_trajectory_output(directory, filename, columns):
    """Load and validate one per-frame endpoint (analyses B-E)."""
    header, rows = read_csv_table(directory, filename)
    if list(header) != list(columns):
        raise TableError("%s: header must be exactly %s"
                         % (filename, list(columns)))
    if not rows:
        raise TableError("%s: file has no data rows" % filename)
    n_columns = len(columns)
    frames = []
    values = []
    for position, row in enumerate(rows):
        if len(row) != n_columns:
            raise TableError("%s: data row %d has %d fields, expected %d"
                             % (filename, position + 1, len(row), n_columns))
        frame_value = parse_number(row[0])
        if frame_value is None:
            raise TableError("%s: data row %d: frame %r is not a finite number"
                             % (filename, position + 1, row[0]))
        frame = int(frame_value)
        if frame != frame_value:
            raise TableError("%s: data row %d: frame %r is not an integer"
                             % (filename, position + 1, row[0]))
        frames.append(frame)
        row_values = []
        for index in range(1, n_columns):
            cell = row[index]
            value = parse_number(cell)
            if value is None:
                raise TableError(
                    "%s: data row %d, column %r: %r is not a finite number"
                    % (filename, position + 1, columns[index], cell))
            row_values.append(value)
        values.append(row_values)
    if frames != list(range(len(frames))):
        raise TableError(
            "%s: frame column must be the complete strictly increasing "
            "0-based frame series 0..%d (one row per trajectory frame)"
            % (filename, len(rows) - 1))
    return frames, values


def check_open_closed(reference_dir, submission_dir):
    reference_value = load_single_output(reference_dir)
    submission_value = load_single_output(submission_dir)
    if submission_value < 0:
        return False, ("rmsd_backbone_angstrom = %.12g is negative; RMSD "
                       "values must be nonnegative" % submission_value)
    deviation = abs(submission_value - reference_value)
    if deviation > allowance(reference_value):
        return False, ("rmsd_backbone_angstrom = %.12g deviates from the "
                      "reference by %.3g A, exceeding the accepted %.3g A"
                      % (submission_value, deviation,
                         allowance(reference_value)))
    return True, ("single value agrees with the reference within the "
                  "accepted bound (%.3g A)" % allowance(reference_value))


def check_trajectory_output(reference_dir, submission_dir, filename, columns):
    ref_frames, ref_values = load_trajectory_output(reference_dir, filename,
                                                    columns)
    sub_frames, sub_values = load_trajectory_output(submission_dir, filename,
                                                     columns)
    if len(sub_frames) != len(ref_frames):
        return False, ("%s: expected %d data rows (one per trajectory "
                       "frame), found %d"
                       % (filename, len(ref_frames), len(sub_frames)))
    value_columns = columns[1:]
    for row_index in range(len(ref_frames)):
        frame = ref_frames[row_index]
        for column_index, column in enumerate(value_columns):
            reference = ref_values[row_index][column_index]
            value = sub_values[row_index][column_index]
            if value < 0:
                return False, ("%s: frame %d, column %s: value %.12g is "
                               "negative; RMSD values must be nonnegative"
                               % (filename, frame, column, value))
            deviation = abs(value - reference)
            if deviation > allowance(reference):
                return False, ("%s: frame %d, column %s: value %.12g deviates "
                               "from the reference by %.3g A, exceeding the "
                               "accepted %.3g A"
                               % (filename, frame, column, value, deviation,
                                  allowance(reference)))
    return True, ("%s: header, all %d frames and all %d value columns agree "
                  "with the reference"
                  % (filename, len(ref_frames), len(value_columns)))


def check_frame_series(reference_dir, submission_dir):
    reference_series = None
    for filename, columns in TRAJECTORY_OUTPUTS:
        frames, _ = load_trajectory_output(reference_dir, filename, columns)
        if reference_series is None:
            reference_series = frames
        elif frames != reference_series:
            raise TableError("%s: reference frame series is inconsistent "
                             "with the other reference tables" % filename)
    for filename, columns in TRAJECTORY_OUTPUTS:
        frames, _ = load_trajectory_output(submission_dir, filename, columns)
        if frames != reference_series:
            return False, ("%s: frame series does not match the shared frame "
                           "series of the trajectory tables" % filename)
    return True, ("all four trajectory tables carry the identical complete "
                  "0-based frame series")


def grade(reference_dir, submission_dir):
    check_functions = [
        ("open_closed_rmsd", check_open_closed),
        ("backbone_fit_domain_rmsd",
         lambda ref, sub: check_trajectory_output(ref, sub,
                                                   *TRAJECTORY_OUTPUTS[0])),
        ("ca_core_rmsd",
         lambda ref, sub: check_trajectory_output(ref, sub,
                                                   *TRAJECTORY_OUTPUTS[1])),
        ("mass_weighted_rmsd",
         lambda ref, sub: check_trajectory_output(ref, sub,
                                                   *TRAJECTORY_OUTPUTS[2])),
        ("resid_weighted_rmsd",
         lambda ref, sub: check_trajectory_output(ref, sub,
                                                   *TRAJECTORY_OUTPUTS[3])),
        ("trajectory_frame_series", check_frame_series),
    ]
    results = []
    for check_id, func in check_functions:
        try:
            passed, message = func(reference_dir, submission_dir)
        except TableError as exc:
            passed, message = False, str(exc)
        except Exception as exc:  # defensive: the grader must not crash
            passed, message = False, "internal grading error: %s" % exc
        results.append({"id": check_id, "passed": bool(passed),
                        "message": str(message)})
    return results


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        description="Grade the adenylate-kinase RMSD task outputs.")
    parser.add_argument("--reference-dir", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--submission-dir", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--report", required=True)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    checks = grade(args.reference_dir, args.submission_dir)
    report = {"passed": all(entry["passed"] for entry in checks),
              "checks": checks}
    with open(args.report, "w", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
        json.dump(report, handle)
        handle.write("\n")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Reference solution for the AdK open<->closed RMSD task.

Solves the public task using only the supplied inputs/ directory and writes
the five required CSV tables to the given output directory.
"""
import argparse
import os

import MDAnalysis as mda
import pandas as pd
from MDAnalysis.analysis import rms

CORE = 'backbone and (resid 1-29 or resid 60-121 or resid 160-214)'
LID = 'backbone and resid 122-159'
NMP = 'backbone and resid 30-59'


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="AdK RMSD analyses A-E")
    ap.add_argument('--input-dir', required=True)
    ap.add_argument('--output-dir', required=True)
    args = ap.parse_args()

    psf = os.path.join(args.input_dir, 'adk.psf')
    dcd = os.path.join(args.input_dir, 'adk_trajectory.dcd')
    crd = os.path.join(args.input_dir, 'adk_open.crd')
    os.makedirs(args.output_dir, exist_ok=True)

    u = mda.Universe(psf, dcd)        # trajectory (frame 0 = closed)
    ref_open = mda.Universe(psf, crd)  # open conformation

    # ---- A. Open vs closed endpoint backbone RMSD ----------------------
    a_value = float(rms.rmsd(u.select_atoms('backbone').positions,
                             ref_open.select_atoms('backbone').positions,
                             center=True,
                             superposition=True))
    pd.DataFrame({'rmsd_backbone_angstrom': [a_value]}).to_csv(
        os.path.join(args.output_dir, 'rmsd_backbone_open_closed.csv'),
        index=False)

    # ---- B. Backbone fit, CORE/LID/NMP residual group RMSDs -------------
    R = rms.RMSD(u, u,
                 select='backbone',
                 groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP],
                 ref_frame=0)
    R.run()
    b = R.results.rmsd
    pd.DataFrame({'frame': b[:, 0].astype(int),
                  'rmsd_backbone_angstrom': b[:, 2],
                  'rmsd_core_angstrom': b[:, 3],
                  'rmsd_lid_angstrom': b[:, 4],
                  'rmsd_nmp_angstrom': b[:, 5]}).to_csv(
        os.path.join(args.output_dir, 'rmsd_backbone_domains.csv'),
        index=False)

    # ---- C. CORE restricted to alpha-carbons ----------------------------
    ca = u.select_atoms('name CA')
    Rc = rms.RMSD(ca, ca, select=CORE, ref_frame=0)
    Rc.run()
    c = Rc.results.rmsd
    pd.DataFrame({'frame': c[:, 0].astype(int),
                  'rmsd_core_ca_angstrom': c[:, 2]}).to_csv(
        os.path.join(args.output_dir, 'rmsd_ca_core.csv'),
        index=False)

    # ---- D. Mass-weighted ------------------------------------------------
    Rd = rms.RMSD(u, u,
                  select='protein and name CA',
                  weights='mass',
                  groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP])
    Rd.run()
    d = Rd.results.rmsd
    pd.DataFrame({'frame': d[:, 0].astype(int),
                  'rmsd_ca_mass_angstrom': d[:, 2],
                  'rmsd_core_mass_angstrom': d[:, 3],
                  'rmsd_lid_mass_angstrom': d[:, 4],
                  'rmsd_nmp_mass_angstrom': d[:, 5]}).to_csv(
        os.path.join(args.output_dir, 'rmsd_mass_weighted.csv'),
        index=False)

    # ---- E. Residue-number-weighted ---------------------------------------
    ag = u.select_atoms('protein and name CA')
    core = u.select_atoms(CORE)
    lid = u.select_atoms(LID)
    nmp = u.select_atoms(NMP)
    Re = rms.RMSD(u, u,
                  select='protein and name CA',
                  groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP],
                  weights=ag.resids,
                  weights_groupselections=[core.resids,
                                           lid.resids,
                                           nmp.resids])
    Re.run()
    e = Re.results.rmsd
    pd.DataFrame({'frame': e[:, 0].astype(int),
                  'rmsd_ca_resid_angstrom': e[:, 2],
                  'rmsd_core_resid_angstrom': e[:, 3],
                  'rmsd_lid_resid_angstrom': e[:, 4],
                  'rmsd_nmp_resid_angstrom': e[:, 5]}).to_csv(
        os.path.join(args.output_dir, 'rmsd_resid_weighted.csv'),
        index=False)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

  • Extra text before or after the JSON will generate warnings but be tolerated

  • Commands array can be empty if you want to wait without taking action

Task Description:

Task: RMSD analysis of the adenylate kinase open↔closed transition

Adenylate kinase (AdK) has a stable CORE domain flanked by the LID and NMP domains, which move as the enzyme transitions between closed and open conformations. You are supplied with the topology, a trajectory sampling the closed→open transition, and the open-conformation coordinates. Quantify this conformational change by computing the root mean square deviation (RMSD) of atomic positions, in Angstrom, in five analyses below.

Supplied inputs

  • inputs/adk.psf — protein topology (PSF) for the AdK structure; 214 residues with atom counts and atom order shared by all supplied coordinate data.
  • inputs/adk_trajectory.dcd — trajectory (DCD) sampling the closed→open transition.
  • inputs/adk_open.crd — coordinates (CRD) of the open conformation of the same structure.

Definitions

For coordinate arrays x (one row per atom, atoms in matching order between compared structures) and reference x^(ref):

  • RMSD(x, x^(ref)) = sqrt( (1/n) Σᵢ |xᵢ − xᵢ^(ref)|² )
  • Weighted RMSD(x, x^(ref)) = sqrt( Σᵢ wᵢ |xᵢ − xᵢ^(ref)|² / Σᵢ wᵢ ) (invariant to any overall positive scaling of the weights).
  • Optimal superposition: the displacement / rotation pair that minimizes the (weighted) RMSD; rotations are proper (determinant +1). RMSD under optimal superposition is the minimum over such pairs, with coordinates first expressed relative to the appropriate weighted centroid.
  • Backbone atoms: the main-chain protein atoms (N, CA, C, O).
  • Domains (residue numbers as in the topology):
    • CORE = backbone atoms of residues 1–29, 60–121, 160–214
    • LID = backbone atoms of residues 122–159
    • NMP = backbone atoms of residues 30–59

Required analyses

A. Open vs. closed endpoint conformations. RMSD between the backbone atoms of the open structure (adk_open.crd) and the trajectory's first frame (closed conformation). Subtract the center of geometry of each set, apply optimal superposition, and report the resulting backbone RMSD.

B–E. Trajectory RMSD versus frame 0. For each of the analyses below, the reference is frame 0 of the trajectory itself. For each trajectory frame, first superimpose the frame onto frame 0 by the optimal (weighted, where weights are specified) rigid-body transformation determined by the fitting group; then report:

  1. the RMSD of the fitting group under that fit; and
  2. for each listed domain group, the RMSD between the frame's transformed coordinates and the untransformed frame-0 coordinates of that group's atoms, computed without any further fitting, centering, or re-alignment of the group (the group RMSD measures residual domain displacement under the single global superposition).

B. Backbone and domains (unweighted). Fitting group: all backbone atoms, unweighted. Report four series: backbone (under the fit), CORE, LID, NMP (group RMSDs, unweighted). Group atom sets are the backbone atoms of the full structure given by the domain definitions above.

C. CORE restricted to alpha-carbons. Restrict the entire analysis to the alpha-carbon (CA) atoms. Fitting group: the alpha-carbons of the CORE domain. Report the CORE fit RMSD.

D. Mass-weighted. Fitting group: all alpha-carbons of the protein, with each atom weighted by its mass (mass-weighted centroids for the superposition). Report the mass-weighted fit RMSD for the alpha-carbons, and mass-weighted group RMSDs for CORE, LID, NMP. Group atom sets are the backbone atoms of the full structure (not restricted to alpha-carbons), and the group RMSDs are also mass-weighted (each atom weighted by its mass).

E. Residue-number-weighted. Same structure as D, but each atom is weighted by its residue number instead of its mass — in the fitting group (alpha-carbons of the protein) and in the CORE, LID, NMP group RMSDs (backbone atoms, full structure, weighted by residue number).

Note that in D and E the fitting group and the reported group RMSDs use the specified weighting; the groups being compared are the full-structure backbone atom sets, independent of the alpha-carbon restriction on the fitting group.

Required outputs

Write CSV files (UTF-8, one header row, comma-separated) under outputs/. All RMSD values are in Angstrom and must be finite. Each trajectory table contains exactly one row per trajectory frame, ordered by strictly increasing frame index (the row order is the time series). The frame column is the 0-based trajectory frame index. Do not output a time column.

  1. outputs/rmsd_backbone_open_closed.csv — analysis A. Columns: rmsd_backbone_angstrom. One data row.
  2. outputs/rmsd_backbone_domains.csv — analysis B. Columns: frame, rmsd_backbone_angstrom, rmsd_core_angstrom, rmsd_lid_angstrom, rmsd_nmp_angstrom.
  3. outputs/rmsd_ca_core.csv — analysis C. Columns: frame, rmsd_core_ca_angstrom.
  4. outputs/rmsd_mass_weighted.csv — analysis D. Columns: frame, rmsd_ca_mass_angstrom, rmsd_core_mass_angstrom, rmsd_lid_mass_angstrom, rmsd_nmp_mass_angstrom.
  5. outputs/rmsd_resid_weighted.csv — analysis E. Columns: frame, rmsd_ca_resid_angstrom, rmsd_core_resid_angstrom, rmsd_lid_resid_angstrom, rmsd_nmp_resid_angstrom.

The frame identity is shared across outputs 2–5: each must cover exactly the same set of trajectory frames, once each, in the same order. The RMSD at frame 0 is expected to be near zero (floating-point rounding of identical conformations), not exactly zero.

Environment and limits

CPU-only; no network access; run within 600 seconds and 8 GiB RAM. Software choice is open: any tools may be used as long as the outputs above are produced. For convenience, a compatible offline environment (MDAnalysis 2.11.0, NumPy, pandas) can be supplied; using it is not a requirement.

Acceptance rules

Grading rules (acceptance addendum)

The task question above defines the science. This addendum fixes exactly how submissions are compared. All RMSD quantities are in Angstrom. Software choice is open: any implementation that produces the declared values is acceptable.

1. Declared outputs and paths

Exactly five files are graded, each read at <name> relative to the output root supplied to the grader (in the solution environment this root is /workspace/outputs):

  1. rmsd_backbone_open_closed.csv — analysis A
  2. rmsd_backbone_domains.csv — analysis B
  3. rmsd_ca_core.csv — analysis C
  4. rmsd_mass_weighted.csv — analysis D
  5. rmsd_resid_weighted.csv — analysis E

A file present only under an additional directory layer below the output root (e.g. a further outputs/ subdirectory) is not at its declared path and counts as missing. Undeclared extra files are ignored.

2. CSV structure (each file)

  • UTF-8 text, comma-separated values, exactly one header row followed by data rows. LF or CRLF line endings are both accepted.
  • The header must be exactly the published column list for that file — same names, same order; no missing, extra, renamed or reordered columns (in particular, no time column).
  • Every data row must contain exactly one field per header column. Blank, ragged or padded rows fail. A file with no data row fails.
  • Every field (in all columns, including frame) must parse as a single finite decimal number: optional sign, optional decimal point, optional exponent notation. Empty fields and NaN/Inf (any case) fail. A cell of the exact form np.float64(<finite number>) is also accepted and read as the enclosed number. RMSD values must be nonnegative; frame values must be integers.
  • rmsd_backbone_open_closed.csv must contain exactly one data row.
  • Each of outputs 2–5 must contain exactly one data row per trajectory frame: the frame column holds the complete 0-based index series 0, 1, …, F−1, each frame exactly once, in strictly increasing order, so that row k carries frame k. Missing, duplicated, out-of-order or non-contiguous frames fail. The required row count F is the number of frames of the supplied trajectory and is taken from the reference tables, not from the submission.
  • Outputs 2–5 must present the same frame series (identical set, identical order, identical count); this cross-table frame identity is checked separately.

3. Numeric comparison

Each submission value is compared to the reference value of the same file, the same column and the same frame index (for output 1, its single value), one-to-one by row. Coverage, order and multiplicity all matter: rows are never compared as a set, and a table that drops, adds, duplicates or reorders rows fails. With submission value v and reference value r:

PASS  if and only if  |v − r| ≤ 1×10⁻⁵ + 1×10⁻⁹ × |r|

The relative term uses the reference value as its denominator. The bound is inclusive and must hold for every value cell of the file.

Tolerance basis: the reference tables are computed in double precision from the supplied inputs. At frame 0 the reference itself carries only the floating-point self-RMSD rounding of identical conformations (below about 1×10⁻⁶ Å in every recorded reference table; the task question itself states the frame-0 RMSD is near-zero rounding, not exactly zero), so a submission reporting exactly 0 — or its own equivalent rounding noise — at frame 0 passes through the absolute term. The absolute term 1×10⁻⁵ Å is at least an order of magnitude above that rounding scale; it also covers faithful double-precision recomputation as demonstrated by controls: an independently implemented weighted-Kabsch optimal-superposition recomputation passed every value comparison within this bound (its author additionally reports, but the executed controls alone do not establish, far closer spot-check agreement), and decimal text rounding is bounded by 5×10⁻⁶ Å at 5 decimal places, which still passes, while about 4 or fewer decimals can fail for values near these tables' upper range (several Å). Executed wrong submissions demonstrate the bound's low end of rejection: a deliberately off-tolerance 2×10⁻⁵ Å perturbation and the executed wrong-method variants, with deviations from roughly 1×10⁻³ Å up to several Å, all fail with clear margin. The bound is a limit on observable output differences, not a guarantee that every wrong method is detected in every cell: a value wrong by less than 1×10⁻⁵ Å + 1×10⁻⁹|r| in a given cell passes by construction, and different weighting schemes can agree to about 1×10⁻⁷ Å at frame 0. Textual formatting (digit count, exponent style, trailing zeros, quoted or plain number text) is free as long as the parsed values satisfy the rule.

Each file is graded independently; any single failing value, row or structural defect fails that file's check, and overall acceptance is the conjunction of all checks.

Task directories

Read the supplied inputs from /workspace/inputs/. Write all required output files under /workspace/outputs/, using the relative filenames specified above. The working directory is /workspace. Aliases /inputs/ and /outputs/ refer to these same directories.

import MDAnalysis as mda
import numpy as np
u=mda.Universe('/workspace/inputs/adk.psf','/workspace/inputs/adk_trajectory.dcd')
names=u.atoms.names; resids=u.atoms.resids
bb=np.isin(names,['N','CA','C','O'])
ca=names=='CA'
ranges=[(1,29),(60,121),(160,214),(122,159),(30,59)]
print('backbone atoms:',bb.sum(),'CA atoms:',ca.sum())
for a,b in ranges:
    domain=(resids>=a)&(resids<=b)
    print(f'residues {a:3d}-{b:3d}: backbone={np.sum(bb&domain):3d}, CA={np.sum(ca&domain):3d}')
print('total domain backbone:',sum(np.sum(bb&((resids>=a)&(resids<=b))) for a,b in ranges))

/opt/venv/bin/python - <<'PY'
import numpy as np
rng=np.random.default_rng(12345)
Y=rng.normal(size=(100,3))
# QR gives a random proper rotation; rotate row coordinates by Q.T (column form Q)
Q,_=np.linalg.qr(rng.normal(size=(3,3)))
if np.linalg.det(Q)<0: Q[:,2]*=-1
X=Y@Q.T
w=rng.uniform(.1,3,size=100)
cx=np.average(X,axis=0,weights=w); cy=np.average(Y,axis=0,weights=w)
Xc=X-cx; Yc=Y-cy
H=Xc.T@(w[:,None]*Yc)
U,S,Vt=np.linalg.svd(H)
R=U@Vt
if np.linalg.det(R)<0:
    Vt[-1,:]*=-1
    R=U@Vt
Xfit=Xc@R+cy
err=np.sqrt(np.average(np.sum((Xfit-Y)**2,axis=1),weights=w))
print('det(R)=',np.linalg.det(R))
print('R vs inverse rotation max abs =',np.max(np.abs(R-Q)))
print('weighted RMSD =',err)
PY
