    "candidate/pyproject.toml": "[project]\nname = \"mdanalysis-rmsd-reference\"\nversion = \"0.1.0\"\nrequires-python = \">=3.13\"\ndependencies = [\n    \"MDAnalysis==2.11.0\",\n    \"MDAnalysisTests==2.11.0\",\n    \"pandas==3.1.0\",\n    \"matplotlib==3.11.2\",\n]\n",
    "inputs/exports.py": "# --- Export of terminal scientific results ---\n# Save the existing RMSD result tables produced by the original script.\nimport os\n\n_output_dir = \"/work/outputs\"\nos.makedirs(_output_dir, exist_ok=True)\n\ndf.to_csv(os.path.join(_output_dir, \"rmsd_ca_core_domain.csv\"), index=False)\ndf_mass.to_csv(os.path.join(_output_dir, \"rmsd_mass_weighted.csv\"), index=False)\ndf_charge.to_csv(os.path.join(_output_dir, \"rmsd_resid_weighted.csv\"), index=False)",
    "inputs/original.py": "# ---\n# jupyter:\n#   jupytext:\n#     text_representation:\n#       extension: .py\n#       format_name: nomarker\n#       format_version: '1.0'\n#       jupytext_version: 1.19.6\n#   kernelspec:\n#     display_name: guide\n#     language: python\n#     name: python3\n# ---\n\n# # Calculating the root mean square deviation of atomic structures\n#\n# We calculate the RMSD of domains in adenylate kinase as it transitions from an open to closed structure, and look at calculating weighted RMSDs.\n#\n# **Last updated:** December 2022 with MDAnalysis 2.4.0-dev0\n#\n# **Minimum version of MDAnalysis:** 1.0.0\n#\n# **Packages required:**\n#     \n# * MDAnalysis (<a data-cite=\"michaud-agrawal_mdanalysis_2011\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1002/jcc.21787\">Michaud-Agrawal *et al.*, 2011</a>, <a data-cite=\"gowers_mdanalysis_2016\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.25080/Majora-629e541a-00e\">Gowers *et al.*, 2016</a>)\n# * MDAnalysisTests\n# * [pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org)\n#\n# **See also**\n#\n# * [Pairwise (2D) RMSD](pairwise_rmsd.ipynb)\n# * [RMSF](rmsf.ipynb)\n#\n# <div class=\"alert alert-info\">\n#     \n# **Note**\n#\n# MDAnalysis implements RMSD calculation using the fast QCP algorithm (<a data-cite=\"theobald_rapid_2005\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1107/S0108767305015266\">Theobald, 2005</a>). Please cite (<a data-cite=\"theobald_rapid_2005\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1107/S0108767305015266\">Theobald, 2005</a>) when using the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.align`` module in published work.\n#\n# </div>\n\nimport MDAnalysis as mda\nfrom MDAnalysis.tests.datafiles import PSF, DCD, CRD\nfrom MDAnalysis.analysis import rms\n\nimport pandas as pd\n# the next line is necessary to display plots in Jupyter\n# Notebook presentation directive: %matplotlib inline\n\n\n# ## Loading files\n\n# The test files we will be working with here feature adenylate kinase (AdK), a phosophotransferase enzyme. (<a data-cite=\"beckstein_zipping_2009\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmb.2009.09.009\">Beckstein *et al.*, 2009</a>) The trajectory ``DCD`` samples a transition from a closed to an open conformation. AdK has three domains: \n#\n#   * CORE\n#   * LID: an ATP-binding domain\n#   * NMP: an AMP-binding domain\n#   \n# The LID and NMP domains move around the stable CORE as the enzyme transitions between the opened and closed conformations. One way to quantify this movement is by calculating the root mean square deviation (RMSD) of atomic positions.\n\nu = mda.Universe(PSF, DCD)  # closed AdK (PDB ID: 1AKE)\nref = mda.Universe(PSF, CRD)  # open AdK (PDB ID: 4AKE)\n\n# ## Background\n#\n# The root mean square deviation (RMSD) of particle coordinates is one measure of distance, or dissimilarity, between molecular conformations. Each structure should have matching elementwise atoms $i$ in the same order, as the distance between them is calculated and summed for the final result. It is calculated between coordinate arrays $\\mathbf{x}$ and $\\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}$ according to the equation below:\n#\n# $$ \\text{RMSD}(\\mathbf{x}, \\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}) = \\sqrt{\\frac{1}{n} \\sum_{i=1}^{n}{|\\mathbf{x}_i-\\mathbf{x}_i^{\\text{ref}}|^2}} $$\n#\n# As molecules can move around, the structure $\\mathbf{x}$ is usually translated by a vector $\\mathbf{t}$ and rotated by a matrix $\\mathsf{R}$ to align with the reference $\\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}$ such that the RMSD is minimised. The RMSD after this optimal superposition can be expressed as follows:\n#\n# $$ \\text{RMSD}(\\mathbf{x}, \\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}) = \\min_{\\mathsf{R}, \\mathbf{t}} %\n#   \\sqrt{\\frac{1}{N} \\sum_{i=1}^{N} \\left[ %\n#       (\\mathsf{R}\\cdot\\mathbf{x}_{i}(t) + \\mathbf{t}) - \\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\\text{ref}} \\right]^{2}}$$\n#\n# The RMSD between one reference state and a trajectory of structures is often calculated as a way to measure the dissimilarity of the trajectory conformational ensemble to the reference. This reference is frequently the first frame of the trajectory (the default in MDAnalysis), in which case it can provide insight into the overall movement from the initial starting point. While stable RMSD values from a reference structure are frequently used as a measure of conformational convergence, this metric suffers from the problem of *degeneracy*: many different structures can have the same RMSD from the same reference. For an alternative measure, you could use [pairwise or 2D RMSD](pairwise_rmsd.ipynb).\n#\n# Typically not all coordinates in a structures are included in an RMSD analysis. With proteins, the fluctuation of the residue side-chains is not representative of overall conformational change. Therefore when RMSD analyses are performed to investigate large-scale movements in proteins, the atoms are usually restricted only to the backbone atoms (forming the amide-bond chain) or the alpha-carbon atoms. \n#\n# MDAnalysis provides functions and classes to calculate the [RMSD between coordinate arrays](#RMSD-between-two-sets-of-coordinates), and [Universes](#RMSD-of-a-Universe-with-multiple-selections) or [AtomGroups](#RMSD-of-an-AtomGroup-with-multiple-selections). \n#\n# The contribution of each particle $i$ to the final RMSD value can also [be weighted](#Weighted-RMSD-of-a-trajectory) by $w_i$:\n#\n# $$ \\text{RMSD}(\\mathbf{x}, \\mathbf{x}^\\text{ref}) = \\sqrt{\\frac{\\sum_{i=1}^{n}{w_i|\\mathbf{x}_i-\\mathbf{x}_i^{\\text{ref}}|^2}}{\\sum_{i-1}^n w_i}} $$\n#\n# RMSD analyses are frequently weighted by mass. The MDAnalysis RMSD class ([API docs](https://docs.mdanalysis.org/stable/documentation_pages/analysis/rms.html#MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.RMSD)) allows you to both [select mass-weighting](#Mass) with `weights='mass'` or `weights_groupselections='mass'`, or to [pass custom arrays](#Custom-weights) into either keyword.\n\n# ## RMSD between two sets of coordinates\n\n# The ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.rmsd`` function returns the root mean square deviation (in Angstrom) between two sets of coordinates. Here, we calculate the RMSD between the backbone atoms of the open and closed conformations of AdK. Only considering the backbone atoms is often more helpful than calculating the RMSD for all the atoms, as movement in amino acid side-chains isn't indicative of overall conformational change.\n\nrms.rmsd(u.select_atoms('backbone').positions,  # coordinates to align\n         ref.select_atoms('backbone').positions,  # reference coordinates\n         center=True,  # subtract the center of geometry\n         superposition=True)  # superimpose coordinates\n\n# ## RMSD of a Universe with multiple selections\n\n# It is more efficient to use the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.RMSD`` class to calculate the RMSD of an entire trajectory to a single reference point, than to use the the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.rmsd`` function.\n#\n# The ``rms.RMSD`` class first performs a rotational and translational alignment of the target trajectory to the reference universe at ``ref_frame``, using the atoms in ``select`` to determine the transformation. The RMSD of the ``select`` selection is calculated. Then, *without further alignment*, the RMSD of each group in ``groupselections`` is calculated. \n\nCORE = 'backbone and (resid 1-29 or resid 60-121 or resid 160-214)'\nLID = 'backbone and resid 122-159'\nNMP = 'backbone and resid 30-59'\n\nR = rms.RMSD(u,  # universe to align\n             u,  # reference universe or atomgroup\n             select='backbone',  # group to superimpose and calculate RMSD\n             groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP],  # groups for RMSD\n             ref_frame=0)  # frame index of the reference\nR.run()\n\n# The data is saved in ``R.rmsd`` as an array.\n\nR.results.rmsd.shape\n\n# ``R.rmsd`` has a row for each timestep. The first two columns of each row are the frame index of the time step, and the time (which is guessed in trajectory formats without timesteps). The third column is RMSD of ``select``. The last few columns are the RMSD of the groups in ``groupselections``.\n\n# ### Plotting the data\n#\n# We can easily plot this data using the common data analysis package [pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org). We turn the ``R.rmsd`` array into a [DataFrame](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/dsintro.html#dataframe) and label each column below.\n\ndf = pd.DataFrame(R.results.rmsd, \n                  columns=['Frame', 'Time (ns)', \n                           'Backbone', 'CORE', \n                           'LID', 'NMP'])\n\ndf\n\nax = df.plot(x='Frame', y=['Backbone', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'],\n             kind='line')\nax.set_ylabel(r'RMSD ($\\AA$)')\n\n# ## RMSD of an AtomGroup with multiple selections\n#\n# The `RMSD` class accepts both `AtomGroup`s and `Universe`s as arguments. Restricting the atoms considered to an AtomGroup can be very helpful, as the `select` and `groupselections` arguments are applied only to the atoms in the original `AtomGroup`. In the example below, for example, only the alpha-carbons of the CORE domain are incorporated in the analysis.\n#\n# <div class=\"alert alert-info\">\n#     \n# **Note**\n#\n# This feature does not currently support `groupselections`.\n#\n# </div>\n\nca = u.select_atoms('name CA')\n\nR = rms.RMSD(ca, ca, select=CORE, ref_frame=0)\nR.run()\n\ndf = pd.DataFrame(R.results.rmsd, \n                  columns=['Frame', 'Time (ns)', \n                           'CORE'])\n\nax = df.plot(x='Frame', y='CORE', kind='line')\nax.set_ylabel('RMSD ($\\AA$)')\n\n# ## Weighted RMSD of a trajectory\n#\n# You can also calculate the weighted RMSD of a trajectory using the `weights` and `weights_groupselections` keywords. The former only applies weights to the group in `select`, while the latter must be a list of the *same length and order* as `groupselections`. If you would like to only weight certain groups in `groupselections`, use `None` for the unweighted groups. Both `weights` and `weights_groupselections` accept `None` (for unweighted), `'mass'` (to weight by mass), and custom arrays. A custom array should have the same number of values as there are particles in the corresponding AtomGroup.\n\n# ### Mass\n\n# It is common to weight RMSD analyses by particle weight, so the `RMSD` class accepts `'mass'` as an argument for `weights`. Note that the `weights` keyword only applies to the group in `select`, and does not apply to the `groupselections`; these remain unweighted below.\n\nR_mass = rms.RMSD(u, u,\n                  select='protein and name CA',\n                  weights='mass',\n                  groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP])\nR_mass.run()\n\n# The plot looks largely the same as above because all the alpha-carbons and individual backbone atoms have the same mass. Below we show how you can pass in custom weights.\n\ndf_mass = pd.DataFrame(R_mass.results.rmsd, \n                       columns=['Frame', \n                                'Time (ns)', \n                                'C-alphas', 'CORE', \n                                'LID', 'NMP'])\nax_mass = df_mass.plot(x='Frame', \n                       y=['C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'])\nax_mass.set_ylabel('Mass-weighted RMSD ($\\AA$)')\n\n# ### Custom weights\n\n# You can also pass in an array of values for the weights. This must have the same length as the number of atoms in your selection groups. In this example, we pass in arrays of residue numbers. This **is not a typical weighting you might choose**, but we use it here to show how you can get different results to the previous graphs for mass-weighted and non-weighted RMSD. You could choose to pass in an array of charges, or your own custom value. \n#\n# First we select the atom groups to make this easier.\n\nag = u.select_atoms('protein and name CA')\nprint('Shape of C-alpha charges:', ag.charges.shape)\ncore = u.select_atoms(CORE)\nlid = u.select_atoms(LID)\nnmp = u.select_atoms(NMP)\n\n# Below, we pass in weights for `ag` with the `weights` keyword, and weights for the `groupselections` with the `weights_groupselections` keyword.\n\nR_charge = rms.RMSD(u, u,\n                    select='protein and name CA',\n                    groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP],\n                    weights=ag.resids,\n                    weights_groupselections=[core.resids, \n                                             lid.resids, \n                                             nmp.resids])\nR_charge.run()\n\n# You can see in the below graph that the NMP domain has much higher RMSD than before, as each particle is weighted by its residue number. Conversely, the CORE domain doesn't really change much. We could potentially infer from this that residues later in the NMP domain (with a higher residue number) are mobile during the length of the trajectory, whereas residues later in the CORE domain do not seem to contribute significantly to the RMSD.\n#\n# However, again, this is a **very non-conventional metric** and is shown here simply to demonstrate how to use the code.\n\ndf_charge = pd.DataFrame(R_charge.results.rmsd, \n                         columns=['Frame', \n                                'Time (ns)', \n                                'C-alphas', 'CORE', \n                                'LID', 'NMP'])\nax_charge = df_charge.plot(x='Frame',\n                           y=['C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'])\nax_charge.set_ylabel('Charge-weighted RMSD ($\\AA$)')\n\n# ## References\n#\n# [1] Oliver Beckstein, Elizabeth&nbsp;J. Denning, Juan&nbsp;R. Perilla, and Thomas&nbsp;B.     "trial/reference.py": "# ---\n# jupyter:\n#   jupytext:\n#     text_representation:\n#       extension: .py\n#       format_name: nomarker\n#       format_version: '1.0'\n#       jupytext_version: 1.19.6\n#   kernelspec:\n#     display_name: guide\n#     language: python\n#     name: python3\n# ---\n\n# # Calculating the root mean square deviation of atomic structures\n#\n# We calculate the RMSD of domains in adenylate kinase as it transitions from an open to closed structure, and look at calculating weighted RMSDs.\n#\n# **Last updated:** December 2022 with MDAnalysis 2.4.0-dev0\n#\n# **Minimum version of MDAnalysis:** 1.0.0\n#\n# **Packages required:**\n#     \n# * MDAnalysis (<a data-cite=\"michaud-agrawal_mdanalysis_2011\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1002/jcc.21787\">Michaud-Agrawal *et al.*, 2011</a>, <a data-cite=\"gowers_mdanalysis_2016\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.25080/Majora-629e541a-00e\">Gowers *et al.*, 2016</a>)\n# * MDAnalysisTests\n# * [pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org)\n#\n# **See also**\n#\n# * [Pairwise (2D) RMSD](pairwise_rmsd.ipynb)\n# * [RMSF](rmsf.ipynb)\n#\n# <div class=\"alert alert-info\">\n#     \n# **Note**\n#\n# MDAnalysis implements RMSD calculation using the fast QCP algorithm (<a data-cite=\"theobald_rapid_2005\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1107/S0108767305015266\">Theobald, 2005</a>). Please cite (<a data-cite=\"theobald_rapid_2005\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1107/S0108767305015266\">Theobald, 2005</a>) when using the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.align`` module in published work.\n#\n# </div>\n\nimport MDAnalysis as mda\nfrom MDAnalysis.tests.datafiles import PSF, DCD, CRD\nfrom MDAnalysis.analysis import rms\n\nimport pandas as pd\n# the next line is necessary to display plots in Jupyter\n# Notebook presentation directive: %matplotlib inline\n\n\n# ## Loading files\n\n# The test files we will be working with here feature adenylate kinase (AdK), a phosophotransferase enzyme. (<a data-cite=\"beckstein_zipping_2009\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmb.2009.09.009\">Beckstein *et al.*, 2009</a>) The trajectory ``DCD`` samples a transition from a closed to an open conformation. AdK has three domains: \n#\n#   * CORE\n#   * LID: an ATP-binding domain\n#   * NMP: an AMP-binding domain\n#   \n# The LID and NMP domains move around the stable CORE as the enzyme transitions between the opened and closed conformations. One way to quantify this movement is by calculating the root mean square deviation (RMSD) of atomic positions.\n\nu = mda.Universe(PSF, DCD)  # closed AdK (PDB ID: 1AKE)\nref = mda.Universe(PSF, CRD)  # open AdK (PDB ID: 4AKE)\n\n# ## Background\n#\n# The root mean square deviation (RMSD) of particle coordinates is one measure of distance, or dissimilarity, between molecular conformations. Each structure should have matching elementwise atoms $i$ in the same order, as the distance between them is calculated and summed for the final result. It is calculated between coordinate arrays $\\mathbf{x}$ and $\\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}$ according to the equation below:\n#\n# $$ \\text{RMSD}(\\mathbf{x}, \\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}) = \\sqrt{\\frac{1}{n} \\sum_{i=1}^{n}{|\\mathbf{x}_i-\\mathbf{x}_i^{\\text{ref}}|^2}} $$\n#\n# As molecules can move around, the structure $\\mathbf{x}$ is usually translated by a vector $\\mathbf{t}$ and rotated by a matrix $\\mathsf{R}$ to align with the reference $\\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}$ such that the RMSD is minimised. The RMSD after this optimal superposition can be expressed as follows:\n#\n# $$ \\text{RMSD}(\\mathbf{x}, \\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}) = \\min_{\\mathsf{R}, \\mathbf{t}} %\n#   \\sqrt{\\frac{1}{N} \\sum_{i=1}^{N} \\left[ %\n#       (\\mathsf{R}\\cdot\\mathbf{x}_{i}(t) + \\mathbf{t}) - \\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\\text{ref}} \\right]^{2}}$$\n#\n# The RMSD between one reference state and a trajectory of structures is often calculated as a way to measure the dissimilarity of the trajectory conformational ensemble to the reference. This reference is frequently the first frame of the trajectory (the default in MDAnalysis), in which case it can provide insight into the overall movement from the initial starting point. While stable RMSD values from a reference structure are frequently used as a measure of conformational convergence, this metric suffers from the problem of *degeneracy*: many different structures can have the same RMSD from the same reference. For an alternative measure, you could use [pairwise or 2D RMSD](pairwise_rmsd.ipynb).\n#\n# Typically not all coordinates in a structures are included in an RMSD analysis. With proteins, the fluctuation of the residue side-chains is not representative of overall conformational change. Therefore when RMSD analyses are performed to investigate large-scale movements in proteins, the atoms are usually restricted only to the backbone atoms (forming the amide-bond chain) or the alpha-carbon atoms. \n#\n# MDAnalysis provides functions and classes to calculate the [RMSD between coordinate arrays](#RMSD-between-two-sets-of-coordinates), and [Universes](#RMSD-of-a-Universe-with-multiple-selections) or [AtomGroups](#RMSD-of-an-AtomGroup-with-multiple-selections). \n#\n# The contribution of each particle $i$ to the final RMSD value can also [be weighted](#Weighted-RMSD-of-a-trajectory) by $w_i$:\n#\n# $$ \\text{RMSD}(\\mathbf{x}, \\mathbf{x}^\\text{ref}) = \\sqrt{\\frac{\\sum_{i=1}^{n}{w_i|\\mathbf{x}_i-\\mathbf{x}_i^{\\text{ref}}|^2}}{\\sum_{i-1}^n w_i}} $$\n#\n# RMSD analyses are frequently weighted by mass. The MDAnalysis RMSD class ([API docs](https://docs.mdanalysis.org/stable/documentation_pages/analysis/rms.html#MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.RMSD)) allows you to both [select mass-weighting](#Mass) with `weights='mass'` or `weights_groupselections='mass'`, or to [pass custom arrays](#Custom-weights) into either keyword.\n\n# ## RMSD between two sets of coordinates\n\n# The ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.rmsd`` function returns the root mean square deviation (in Angstrom) between two sets of coordinates. Here, we calculate the RMSD between the backbone atoms of the open and closed conformations of AdK. Only considering the backbone atoms is often more helpful than calculating the RMSD for all the atoms, as movement in amino acid side-chains isn't indicative of overall conformational change.\n\nrms.rmsd(u.select_atoms('backbone').positions,  # coordinates to align\n         ref.select_atoms('backbone').positions,  # reference coordinates\n         center=True,  # subtract the center of geometry\n         superposition=True)  # superimpose coordinates\n\n# ## RMSD of a Universe with multiple selections\n\n# It is more efficient to use the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.RMSD`` class to calculate the RMSD of an entire trajectory to a single reference point, than to use the the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.rmsd`` function.\n#\n# The ``rms.RMSD`` class first performs a rotational and translational alignment of the target trajectory to the reference universe at ``ref_frame``, using the atoms in ``select`` to determine the transformation. The RMSD of the ``select`` selection is calculated. Then, *without further alignment*, the RMSD of each group in ``groupselections`` is calculated. \n\nCORE = 'backbone and (resid 1-29 or resid 60-121 or resid 160-214)'\nLID = 'backbone and resid 122-159'\nNMP = 'backbone and resid 30-59'\n\nR = rms.RMSD(u,  # universe to align\n             u,  # reference universe or atomgroup\n             select='backbone',  # group to superimpose and calculate RMSD\n             groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP],  # groups for RMSD\n             ref_frame=0)  # frame index of the reference\nR.run()\n\n# The data is saved in ``R.rmsd`` as an array.\n\nR.results.rmsd.shape\n\n# ``R.rmsd`` has a row for each timestep. The first two columns of each row are the frame index of the time step, and the time (which is guessed in trajectory formats without timesteps). The third column is RMSD of ``select``. The last few columns are the RMSD of the groups in ``groupselections``.\n\n# ### Plotting the data\n#\n# We can easily plot this data using the common data analysis package [pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org). We turn the ``R.rmsd`` array into a [DataFrame](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/dsintro.html#dataframe) and label each column below.\n\ndf = pd.DataFrame(R.results.rmsd, \n                  columns=['Frame', 'Time (ns)', \n                           'Backbone', 'CORE', \n                           'LID', 'NMP'])\n\ndf\n\nax = df.plot(x='Frame', y=['Backbone', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'],\n             kind='line')\nax.set_ylabel(r'RMSD ($\\AA$)')\n\n# ## RMSD of an AtomGroup with multiple selections\n#\n# The `RMSD` class accepts both `AtomGroup`s and `Universe`s as arguments. Restricting the atoms considered to an AtomGroup can be very helpful, as the `select` and `groupselections` arguments are applied only to the atoms in the original `AtomGroup`. In the example below, for example, only the alpha-carbons of the CORE domain are incorporated in the analysis.\n#\n# <div class=\"alert alert-info\">\n#     \n# **Note**\n#\n# This feature does not currently support `groupselections`.\n#\n# </div>\n\nca = u.select_atoms('name CA')\n\nR = rms.RMSD(ca, ca, select=CORE, ref_frame=0)\nR.run()\n\ndf = pd.DataFrame(R.results.rmsd, \n                  columns=['Frame', 'Time (ns)', \n                           'CORE'])\n\nax = df.plot(x='Frame', y='CORE', kind='line')\nax.set_ylabel('RMSD ($\\AA$)')\n\n# ## Weighted RMSD of a trajectory\n#\n# You can also calculate the weighted RMSD of a trajectory using the `weights` and `weights_groupselections` keywords. The former only applies weights to the group in `select`, while the latter must be a list of the *same length and order* as `groupselections`. If you would like to only weight certain groups in `groupselections`, use `None` for the unweighted groups. Both `weights` and `weights_groupselections` accept `None` (for unweighted), `'mass'` (to weight by mass), and custom arrays. A custom array should have the same number of values as there are particles in the corresponding AtomGroup.\n\n# ### Mass\n\n# It is common to weight RMSD analyses by particle weight, so the `RMSD` class accepts `'mass'` as an argument for `weights`. Note that the `weights` keyword only applies to the group in `select`, and does not apply to the `groupselections`; these remain unweighted below.\n\nR_mass = rms.RMSD(u, u,\n                  select='protein and name CA',\n                  weights='mass',\n                  groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP])\nR_mass.run()\n\n# The plot looks largely the same as above because all the alpha-carbons and individual backbone atoms have the same mass. Below we show how you can pass in custom weights.\n\ndf_mass = pd.DataFrame(R_mass.results.rmsd, \n                       columns=['Frame', \n                                'Time (ns)', \n                                'C-alphas', 'CORE', \n                                'LID', 'NMP'])\nax_mass = df_mass.plot(x='Frame', \n                       y=['C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'])\nax_mass.set_ylabel('Mass-weighted RMSD ($\\AA$)')\n\n# ### Custom weights\n\n# You can also pass in an array of values for the weights. This must have the same length as the number of atoms in your selection groups. In this example, we pass in arrays of residue numbers. This **is not a typical weighting you might choose**, but we use it here to show how you can get different results to the previous graphs for mass-weighted and non-weighted RMSD. You could choose to pass in an array of charges, or your own custom value. \n#\n# First we select the atom groups to make this easier.\n\nag = u.select_atoms('protein and name CA')\nprint('Shape of C-alpha charges:', ag.charges.shape)\ncore = u.select_atoms(CORE)\nlid = u.select_atoms(LID)\nnmp = u.select_atoms(NMP)\n\n# Below, we pass in weights for `ag` with the `weights` keyword, and weights for the `groupselections` with the `weights_groupselections` keyword.\n\nR_charge = rms.RMSD(u, u,\n                    select='protein and name CA',\n                    groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP],\n                    weights=ag.resids,\n                    weights_groupselections=[core.resids, \n                                             lid.resids, \n                                             nmp.resids])\nR_charge.run()\n\n# You can see in the below graph that the NMP domain has much higher RMSD than before, as each particle is weighted by its residue number. Conversely, the CORE domain doesn't really change much. We could potentially infer from this that residues later in the NMP domain (with a higher residue number) are mobile during the length of the trajectory, whereas residues later in the CORE domain do not seem to contribute significantly to the RMSD.\n#\n# However, again, this is a **very non-conventional metric** and is shown here simply to demonstrate how to use the code.\n\ndf_charge = pd.DataFrame(R_charge.results.rmsd, \n                         columns=['Frame', \n                                'Time (ns)', \n                                'C-alphas', 'CORE', \n                                'LID', 'NMP'])\nax_charge = df_charge.plot(x='Frame',\n                           y=['C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'])\nax_charge.set_ylabel('Charge-weighted RMSD ($\\AA$)')\n\n# ## References\n#\n# [1] Oliver Beckstein, Elizabeth&nbsp;J. Denning, Juan&nbsp;R. Perilla, and Thomas&nbsp;B.   "task_brief": "# Task: RMSD analysis of the adenylate kinase open\u2194closed transition\n\nAdenylate kinase (AdK) has a stable CORE domain flanked by the LID and NMP domains, which move as the enzyme transitions between closed and open conformations. You are supplied with the topology, a trajectory sampling the closed\u2192open transition, and the open-conformation coordinates. Quantify this conformational change by computing the root mean square deviation (RMSD) of atomic positions, in Angstrom, in five analyses below.\n\n## Supplied inputs\n\n- `inputs/adk.psf` \u2014 protein topology (PSF) for the AdK structure; 214 residues with atom counts and atom order shared by all supplied coordinate data.\n- `inputs/adk_trajectory.dcd` \u2014 trajectory (DCD) sampling the closed\u2192open transition.\n- `inputs/adk_open.crd` \u2014 coordinates (CRD) of the open conformation of the same structure.\n\n(File byte identities are pinned separately at task setup.)\n\n## Definitions\n\nFor coordinate arrays **x** (one row per atom, atoms in matching order between compared structures) and reference **x**^(ref):\n\n- **RMSD(x, x^(ref)) = sqrt( (1/n) \u03a3\u1d62 |x\u1d62 \u2212 x\u1d62^(ref)|\u00b2 )**\n- **Weighted RMSD(x, x^(ref)) = sqrt( \u03a3\u1d62 w\u1d62 |x\u1d62 \u2212 x\u1d62^(ref)|\u00b2 / \u03a3\u1d62 w\u1d62 )** (invariant to any overall positive scaling of the weights).\n- **Optimal superposition**: the displacement / rotation pair that minimizes the (weighted) RMSD; rotations are proper (determinant +1). RMSD under optimal superposition is the minimum over such pairs, with coordinates first expressed relative to the appropriate weighted centroid.\n- **Backbone atoms**: the main-chain protein atoms (N, CA, C, O).\n- **Domains** (residue numbers as in the topology):\n  - CORE = backbone atoms of residues 1\u201329, 60\u2013121, 160\u2013214\n  - LID = backbone atoms of residues 122\u2013159\n  - NMP = backbone atoms of residues 30\u201359\n\n## Required analyses\n\n**A. Open vs. closed endpoint conformations.** RMSD between the backbone atoms of the open structure (`adk_open.crd`) and the trajectory's first frame (closed conformation). Subtract the center of geometry of each set, apply optimal superposition, and report the resulting backbone RMSD.\n\n**B\u2013E. Trajectory RMSD versus frame 0.** For each of the analyses below, the reference is frame 0 of the trajectory itself. For each trajectory frame, first superimpose the frame onto frame 0 by the optimal (weighted, where weights are specified) rigid-body transformation determined by the fitting group; then report:\n\n1. the RMSD of the fitting group under that fit; and\n2. for each listed domain group, the RMSD between the frame's transformed coordinates and the **untransformed frame-0 coordinates** of that group's atoms, **computed without any further fitting, centering, or re-alignment** of the group (the group RMSD measures residual domain displacement under the single global superposition).\n\n**B. Backbone and domains (unweighted).** Fitting group: all backbone atoms, unweighted. Report four series: backbone (under the fit), CORE, LID, NMP (group RMSDs, unweighted). Group atom sets are the backbone atoms of the full structure given by the domain definitions above.\n\n**C. CORE restricted to alpha-carbons.** Restrict the entire analysis to the alpha-carbon (CA) atoms. Fitting group: the alpha-carbons of the CORE domain. Report the CORE fit RMSD.\n\n**D. Mass-weighted.** Fitting group: all alpha-carbons of the protein, with each atom weighted by its mass (mass-weighted centroids for the superposition). Report the mass-weighted fit RMSD for the alpha-carbons, and mass-weighted group RMSDs for CORE, LID, NMP. Group atom sets are the backbone atoms of the **full structure** (not restricted to alpha-carbons), and the group RMSDs are also mass-weighted (each atom weighted by its mass).\n\n**E. Residue-number-weighted.** Same structure as D, but each atom is weighted by its residue number instead of its mass \u2014 in the fitting group (alpha-carbons of the protein) and in the CORE, LID, NMP group RMSDs (backbone atoms, full structure, weighted by residue number).\n\nNote that in D and E the fitting group and the reported group RMSDs use the specified weighting; the groups being compared are the full-structure backbone atom sets, independent of the alpha-carbon restriction on the fitting group.\n\n## Required outputs\n\nWrite CSV files (UTF-8, one header row, comma-separated). All RMSD values are in Angstrom and must be finite. Each trajectory table contains exactly one row per trajectory frame, ordered by strictly increasing frame index (the row order is the time series). The frame column is the 0-based trajectory frame index. Do not output a time column.\n\n1. `outputs/rmsd_backbone_open_closed.csv` \u2014 analysis A. Columns: `rmsd_backbone_angstrom`. One data row.\n2. `outputs/rmsd_backbone_domains.csv` \u2014 analysis B. Columns: `frame`, `rmsd_backbone_angstrom`, `rmsd_core_angstrom`, `rmsd_lid_angstrom`, `rmsd_nmp_angstrom`.\n3. `outputs/rmsd_ca_core.csv` \u2014 analysis C. Columns: `frame`, `rmsd_core_ca_angstrom`.\n4. `outputs/rmsd_mass_weighted.csv` \u2014 analysis D. Columns: `frame`, `rmsd_ca_mass_angstrom`, `rmsd_core_mass_angstrom`, `rmsd_lid_mass_angstrom`, `rmsd_nmp_mass_angstrom`.\n5. `outputs/rmsd_residue_weighted.csv` \u2014 analysis E. Columns: `frame`, `rmsd_ca_resid_angstrom`, `rmsd_core_resid_angstrom`, `rmsd_lid_resid_angstrom`, `rmsd_nmp_resid_angstrom`.\n\nThe frame identity is shared across outputs 2\u20135: each must cover exactly the same set of trajectory frames, once each, in the same order. The RMSD at frame 0 is expected to be near zero (floating-point rounding of identical conformations), not exactly zero.\n\n## Environment and limits\n\nCPU-only; no network access; run within 600 seconds and 8 GiB RAM. Software choice is open: any tools may be used as long as the outputs above are produced. Proposed question

autonomous-runs/053/explorer-evidence/specification/task-brief.md

Task: RMSD analysis of the adenylate kinase open↔closed transition

Adenylate kinase (AdK) has a stable CORE domain flanked by the LID and NMP domains, which move as the enzyme transitions between closed and open conformations. You are supplied with the topology, a trajectory sampling the closed→open transition, and the open-conformation coordinates. Quantify this conformational change by computing the root mean square deviation (RMSD) of atomic positions, in Angstrom, in five analyses below.

Supplied inputs

  • inputs/adk.psf — protein topology (PSF) for the AdK structure; 214 residues with atom counts and atom order shared by all supplied coordinate data.
  • inputs/adk_trajectory.dcd — trajectory (DCD) sampling the closed→open transition.
  • inputs/adk_open.crd — coordinates (CRD) of the open conformation of the same structure.

(File byte identities are pinned separately at task setup.)

Definitions

For coordinate arrays x (one row per atom, atoms in matching order between compared structures) and reference x^(ref):

  • RMSD(x, x^(ref)) = sqrt( (1/n) Σᵢ |xᵢ − xᵢ^(ref)|² )
  • Weighted RMSD(x, x^(ref)) = sqrt( Σᵢ wᵢ |xᵢ − xᵢ^(ref)|² / Σᵢ wᵢ ) (invariant to any overall positive scaling of the weights).
  • Optimal superposition: the displacement / rotation pair that minimizes the (weighted) RMSD; rotations are proper (determinant +1). RMSD under optimal superposition is the minimum over such pairs, with coordinates first expressed relative to the appropriate weighted centroid.
  • Backbone atoms: the main-chain protein atoms (N, CA, C, O).
  • Domains (residue numbers as in the topology):
    • CORE = backbone atoms of residues 1–29, 60–121, 160–214
    • LID = backbone atoms of residues 122–159
    • NMP = backbone atoms of residues 30–59

Required analyses

A. Open vs. closed endpoint conformations. RMSD between the backbone atoms of the open structure (adk_open.crd) and the trajectory's first frame (closed conformation). Subtract the center of geometry of each set, apply optimal superposition, and report the resulting backbone RMSD.

B–E. Trajectory RMSD versus frame 0. For each of the analyses below, the reference is frame 0 of the trajectory itself. For each trajectory frame, first superimpose the frame onto frame 0 by the optimal (weighted, where weights are specified) rigid-body transformation determined by the fitting group; then report:

  1. the RMSD of the fitting group under that fit; and
  2. for each listed domain group, the RMSD between the frame's transformed coordinates and the untransformed frame-0 coordinates of that group's atoms, computed without any further fitting, centering, or re-alignment of the group (the group RMSD measures residual domain displacement under the single global superposition).

B. Backbone and domains (unweighted). Fitting group: all backbone atoms, unweighted. Report four series: backbone (under the fit), CORE, LID, NMP (group RMSDs, unweighted). Group atom sets are the backbone atoms of the full structure given by the domain definitions above.

C. CORE restricted to alpha-carbons. Restrict the entire analysis to the alpha-carbon (CA) atoms. Fitting group: the alpha-carbons of the CORE domain. Report the CORE fit RMSD.

D. Mass-weighted. Fitting group: all alpha-carbons of the protein, with each atom weighted by its mass (mass-weighted centroids for the superposition). Report the mass-weighted fit RMSD for the alpha-carbons, and mass-weighted group RMSDs for CORE, LID, NMP. Group atom sets are the backbone atoms of the full structure (not restricted to alpha-carbons), and the group RMSDs are also mass-weighted (each atom weighted by its mass).

E. Residue-number-weighted. Same structure as D, but each atom is weighted by its residue number instead of its mass — in the fitting group (alpha-carbons of the protein) and in the CORE, LID, NMP group RMSDs (backbone atoms, full structure, weighted by residue number).

Note that in D and E the fitting group and the reported group RMSDs use the specified weighting; the groups being compared are the full-structure backbone atom sets, independent of the alpha-carbon restriction on the fitting group.

Required outputs

Write CSV files (UTF-8, one header row, comma-separated). All RMSD values are in Angstrom and must be finite. Each trajectory table contains exactly one row per trajectory frame, ordered by strictly increasing frame index (the row order is the time series). The frame column is the 0-based trajectory frame index. Do not output a time column.

  1. outputs/rmsd_backbone_open_closed.csv — analysis A. Columns: rmsd_backbone_angstrom. One data row.
  2. outputs/rmsd_backbone_domains.csv — analysis B. Columns: frame, rmsd_backbone_angstrom, rmsd_core_angstrom, rmsd_lid_angstrom, rmsd_nmp_angstrom.
  3. outputs/rmsd_ca_core.csv — analysis C. Columns: frame, rmsd_core_ca_angstrom.
  4. outputs/rmsd_mass_weighted.csv — analysis D. Columns: frame, rmsd_ca_mass_angstrom, rmsd_core_mass_angstrom, rmsd_lid_mass_angstrom, rmsd_nmp_mass_angstrom.
  5. outputs/rmsd_residue_weighted.csv — analysis E. Columns: frame, rmsd_ca_resid_angstrom, rmsd_core_resid_angstrom, rmsd_lid_resid_angstrom, rmsd_nmp_resid_angstrom.

The frame identity is shared across outputs 2–5: each must cover exactly the same set of trajectory frames, once each, in the same order. The RMSD at frame 0 is expected to be near zero (floating-point rounding of identical conformations), not exactly zero.

Environment and limits

CPU-only; no network access; run within 600 seconds and 8 GiB RAM. Software choice is open: any tools may be used as long as the outputs above are produced. For convenience, a compatible offline environment (MDAnalysis 2.11.0, NumPy, pandas) can be supplied; using it is not a requirement. If you use MDAnalysis, note that its RMSD class's current semantics for weights='mass' (mass applied to group selections as well) match the definitions in D above.

Validation handoff

autonomous-runs/053/explorer-evidence/specification/validation-handoff.md

Proposed scope (not yet fully validated)

Task covers all five eligible endpoints of the executed analysis, two more than the existing exports: the pairwise open-vs-closed backbone RMSD and the first (backbone-wide, unweighted, with CORE/LID/NMP groups) trajectory table. inputs/plan.json excluded these solely because the reference's variable names were overwritten (B) or the expression was unassigned (A); the underlying analyses are fully present in trial/reference.py and executed. Required reference work before solving: re-run the reference with a minimal restructure that assigns distinct names (or exports immediately) so that A (scalar) and B (5-column table) are captured. No new computation is introduced.

Measured facts

  • Reference executed successfully: exit 0, 3.77 s, peak child RSS ~167 MiB (limits: 600 s, 4 CPU, 8 GiB). Offline environment builds and runs.
  • Trajectory has 98 frames; DCD frame time ≈ (frame+1)·dt with dt ≈ 0.9999999119 Å-independent metadata quirk — this is why Time (ns) is excluded from graded outputs.
  • 214 alpha-carbons (execution log). Outputs in output-audit.json are all finite, no ragged rows, one row per frame.
  • Two replay runs were byte-identical — determinism of this build only; no portability or correctness claim.

Methodology verification (pinned source, mdanalysis 2.11.0)

  • MDAnalysis/analysis/rms.py:445-461, 689-711 + MDAnalysis/lib/util.py:1102-1114 (iterable('mass') == False): with weights='mass' and default weights_groupselections=False, group selections are mass-weighted. The notebook narrative ("these remain unweighted") is stale relative to the executed 2.11.0 reference. Public brief pins mass-weighted groups for analysis D.
  • rms.py:770-824: single global fit of select; group RMSDs computed with center=False, superposition=False against raw frame-0 group coordinates (rms.py:733-741); reported select value is the minimal weighted RMSD under the fit (QCP).
  • rms.py:432-440, 618-626: group selections applied to atomgroup.universe.select_atoms(...) — full universe, regardless of any AtomGroup restriction on select. Traps in D/E.
  • rms.py:390-393: defaults weights=None, ref_frame=0 (B/C pass ref_frame=0 explicitly; D/E rely on the default). Weight normalization w/<w'> (rms.py:703-721) is scale-invariant given the Σw denominator, so the public formula is equivalent.

Input materialization (proposed, pending)

  • Stage the AdK data files from the MDAnalysisTests 2.11.0 distribution (datafiles PSF, DCD, CRD) as inputs/adk.psf, inputs/adk_trajectory.dcd, inputs/adk_open.crd; record sha256 identities. Redistribution review is not yet established (provenance.json: "keep biological inputs ... private until checked separately") — publish only after that passes. Solver receives only the three input files and the brief.

Comparison rules (proposed, uncalibrated — no numeric tolerances asserted)

  • Structural: each of outputs 2–5 has one row per trajectory frame (98 expected), frame strictly increasing, no duplicates; same frame set across the four tables under one shared identity mapping. Output 1 = 1 row × 1 value column.
  • Numerical: per-cell RMSD comparison in Å between solver and reference, using max(absolute_component, relative_component) form because frame-0 values are near zero (~1e-7 measured in the audit). Tolerance values must be calibrated by measurement, not assumed: (a) acceptable spread — independent reimplementation of Kabsch/QCP superposition in float64, and re-runs on this stack; (b) unacceptable deviations that must fail — any of: unweighted groups in D (the stale-narrative reading); per-group re-fitting or re-centering in B/D/E; alpha-carbon-restricted group sets in D/E; wrong reference frame; LID/NMP columns swapped; domain residue ranges mis-tiled; missing final-frame rows. Do not adopt a tolerance that admits the unacceptable set.
  • Representation: row order is the time series — require ordered comparison keyed by frame; explicitly include a row-permutation probe that must FAIL. Column names per the brief; numeric formatting free.
  • Cross-file: no cross-table numeric identity is expected except that all tables describe the same frames (identity check only). Note analysis C (CA-only, unweighted) and the CORE column of D (backbone, mass-weighted) are intentionally different quantities.

Open items before finalization

  1. Reference re-run capturing outputs A and B (trivial restructure) and verification that A/B values match the quantities the notebook displays.
  2. Input redistribution clearance and file pinning.
  3. Executable tolerance calibration as above; only then fix grader thresholds.
  4. Solver environment staged offline (pyproject already resolved once; retained uv.lock hash 2f019f7… available).
  5. Confirm no solver-visible answer leakage in the staged inputs (inputs contain no reference-derived content under this design).

Produce the task-specific question and executable artifacts. Here the worker recovered the open/closed and backbone-domain endpoints, preserving all five source analyses.

Program: task_materialization.py

Prompt

Actual system prompt

autonomous-runs/053/explorer-evidence/materialization-raw/materialize/system-prompt.md

Materialize a proposed scientific task from existing evidence

You are a GLM worker building supplied task inputs and a reference solution. Follow the scientific scope in policy and the latest specification. Older exports are evidence, not a requirement to ask the solver for all of them. Do not copy the original function-by-function recipe into the public question.

Submit a complete initial candidate from the supplied source, proposal and recorded observations before using the shell. The controller enforces this ordering: shell commands do not run until a candidate has undergone controlled execution. Use the already executed reference packages and computation for the initial oracle. If execution fails, tool access becomes available to diagnose and repair that demonstrated failure. If the supplied evidence cannot support a candidate, return a concrete blocked disposition instead of inventing missing scientific facts. Successful construction hands off to independent scientific validation; it does not require you to establish numerical equivalence first.

This is construction, not independent scientific validation; a later blind worker performs that check. Prefer adapting the already executed reference implementation. When prior_worker_draft is supplied, reuse its supported code and repair the remaining gaps from source evidence and inspected inputs. Prior execution does not prove its public contract complete. Submit a complete candidate including unchanged fields, rather than rebuilding a separate implementation without a concrete need.

You receive the source, export evidence, replay observations, and the proposed public task together with its private scientific review. draft_ready means a proposal ready for construction, not an approved or validated scientific contract. Read the review before investigating; preserve its established facts and unresolved questions instead of rediscovering them. Notes about later validation are context, not a request to implement that validation here.

Check the proposal against the supplied input observations. Do not assert an input precondition that has not been measured or retain a known unsupported convention solely because the proposal stated it. You may clarify unsupported incidental conventions without changing the scientific target; explain the evidence and each clarification in the rationale. A substantive methodological change requires a blocker, not a silent repair. Leave unresolved numerical equivalence to the comparison stage; do not attempt repeated full independent implementations before submitting a candidate. Grader design and independent-implementation plans belong to later workers. The shell runs in a locked Python environment, offline. /work/reference contains read-only original terminal artifacts. original_inputs identifies read-only original input files and their recorded identities. Work under /work/author. Do not modify or recompute the recorded scientific reference. Avoid redoing its upstream work excluded from the proposed task.

Return a complete structured artifact:

  • instruction: standalone solver question with scientific methods, inputs under inputs/, outputs under outputs/, identifiers, schemas and resource limits. No private paths, measured answer values or exhaustive API recipe. Grading tolerances remain pending validation; do not invent them. Keep pipeline status and pending-validation notes in the private rationale, not the solver question. The controller will append the validated acceptance rules before solving.
  • input_paths, output_paths: relative files inside the respective directories.
  • derive_code: Python CLI accepting --source-inputs PATH (JSON manifest of original absolute paths), --reference-dir PATH (original terminal artifacts), and --destination PATH. Create only destination/inputs/ and destination/reference/. Copy original task data byte-for-byte where required, derive proposed supplied metadata by selecting existing fields, and project selected answer fields from existing reference exports. No new scientific computation or invented answer values. Document provenance in the rationale.
  • oracle_code: Python CLI accepting --input-dir PATH and --output-dir PATH. Solve the public task using only those supplied inputs. It will run under a separate user without access to reference answers or your working directory. Never embed measured answers, access the original reference, or depend on a hidden cache/author artifact. Use the installed environment; no internet.
  • rationale: private explanation of scope, scientific fidelity, input derivation, possible leakage, output projections and remaining comparison questions.

Validate cell/entity alignment explicitly. Prefer original stable identifiers or explicit composite keys for supplied metadata; avoid making the solver reconstruct an incidental package-specific naming convention when a transparent key can be supplied without changing the science. Supplied intermediate results are reference-derived inputs, not biological ground truth. Retain sufficient identity information without exposing downstream answers. Check claimed input formats and headers against the actual staged files. Inspect the actual input keys and output grain, rather than assuming one source row is one scientific entity. When parsing drops records, distinguish verified metadata and scientifically justified selection from unsupported data loss. Never describe a real observation as a header simply because the reference skips it. Report a source-fidelity blocker when the stated population and actual parsing conflict; do not change the source, input bytes or public population merely to reproduce that defect. If the necessary file observations are unavailable, state the evidence gap instead of inventing them. When several source rows share an entity key, check whether their annotations agree. State the intended multiplicity and any rule for selecting or combining conflicting annotations in the public question, supported by the source analysis. Do not leave these as hidden oracle conventions or choose a rule merely to match saved answers; report a blocker if the source and requested task cannot support an explicit rule. Keep the task scientifically substantial. The oracle may use reference packages; the public task does not require those APIs. Do not silently change the requested scientific quantities merely to fit the saved answers. Report a blocker for a genuine incompatibility.

Submit a minimal complete candidate promptly. The controller executes derivation, verifies exact declared inventories and unchanged original input hashes, then runs the oracle from a clean directory for the supplied reference time limit. It returns runtime/schema failures so you can repair your programs. Successful execution alone does not validate numerical equivalence: a separate comparison stage checks the oracle outputs against the projected reference and tests alternatives/errors. Do not spend this stage constructing a grader, a separate clean-room implementation, or a broad mutation suite. Prefer the simplest faithful oracle, normally using the reference packages already installed: adapt the source computation to the proposed scope and supplied inputs. Do not reimplement those packages from statistical primitives in this stage. A fresh worker will independently implement the public question during comparison validation; do not duplicate that stage here. Still report an actual conflict between the public definition and the reference.

Use disposition: ready or blocked; explain blockers in rationale. Tools are shell, submit_artifact and revise_artifact. Do not claim tests you did not run.

Shell execution

Keep diagnostics concise: print aggregate checks and representative examples. Save complete listings to scratch files and inspect selected sections instead of streaming all rows, arrays or mismatches into the conversation.

Where the public question frees row order or textual number formatting, do not reverse-engineer those incidental choices just to match file bytes. A later stage compares scientific content under the validated public contract.

Run commands in the foreground. Each shell call terminates its remaining child processes when it returns; background/nohup work cannot continue between calls. For longer computations, explicitly set timeout_sec up to the supplied reference_seconds limit (the shell default is 120 seconds). Save useful results to files before returning, then inspect them in later calls.

  "source_evidence": {
    "candidate/pyproject.toml": "[project]\nname = \"mdanalysis-rmsd-reference\"\nversion = \"0.1.0\"\nrequires-python = \">=3.13\"\ndependencies = [\n    \"MDAnalysis==2.11.0\",\n    \"MDAnalysisTests==2.11.0\",\n    \"pandas==3.1.0\",\n    \"matplotlib==3.11.2\",\n]\n",
    "inputs/exports.py": "# --- Export of terminal scientific results ---\n# Save the existing RMSD result tables produced by the original script.\nimport os\n\n_output_dir = \"/work/outputs\"\nos.makedirs(_output_dir, exist_ok=True)\n\ndf.to_csv(os.path.join(_output_dir, \"rmsd_ca_core_domain.csv\"), index=False)\ndf_mass.to_csv(os.path.join(_output_dir, \"rmsd_mass_weighted.csv\"), index=False)\ndf_charge.to_csv(os.path.join(_output_dir, \"rmsd_resid_weighted.csv\"), index=False)",
    "inputs/original.py": "# ---\n# jupyter:\n#   jupytext:\n#     text_representation:\n#       extension: .py\n#       format_name: nomarker\n#       format_version: '1.0'\n#       jupytext_version: 1.19.6\n#   kernelspec:\n#     display_name: guide\n#     language: python\n#     name: python3\n# ---\n\n# # Calculating the root mean square deviation of atomic structures\n#\n# We calculate the RMSD of domains in adenylate kinase as it transitions from an open to closed structure, and look at calculating weighted RMSDs.\n#\n# **Last updated:** December 2022 with MDAnalysis 2.4.0-dev0\n#\n# **Minimum version of MDAnalysis:** 1.0.0\n#\n# **Packages required:**\n#     \n# * MDAnalysis (<a data-cite=\"michaud-agrawal_mdanalysis_2011\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1002/jcc.21787\">Michaud-Agrawal *et al.*, 2011</a>, <a data-cite=\"gowers_mdanalysis_2016\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.25080/Majora-629e541a-00e\">Gowers *et al.*, 2016</a>)\n# * MDAnalysisTests\n# * [pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org)\n#\n# **See also**\n#\n# * [Pairwise (2D) RMSD](pairwise_rmsd.ipynb)\n# * [RMSF](rmsf.ipynb)\n#\n# <div class=\"alert alert-info\">\n#     \n# **Note**\n#\n# MDAnalysis implements RMSD calculation using the fast QCP algorithm (<a data-cite=\"theobald_rapid_2005\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1107/S0108767305015266\">Theobald, 2005</a>). Please cite (<a data-cite=\"theobald_rapid_2005\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1107/S0108767305015266\">Theobald, 2005</a>) when using the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.align`` module in published work.\n#\n# </div>\n\nimport MDAnalysis as mda\nfrom MDAnalysis.tests.datafiles import PSF, DCD, CRD\nfrom MDAnalysis.analysis import rms\n\nimport pandas as pd\n# the next line is necessary to display plots in Jupyter\n# Notebook presentation directive: %matplotlib inline\n\n\n# ## Loading files\n\n# The test files we will be working with here feature adenylate kinase (AdK), a phosophotransferase enzyme. (<a data-cite=\"beckstein_zipping_2009\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmb.2009.09.009\">Beckstein *et al.*, 2009</a>) The trajectory ``DCD`` samples a transition from a closed to an open conformation. AdK has three domains: \n#\n#   * CORE\n#   * LID: an ATP-binding domain\n#   * NMP: an AMP-binding domain\n#   \n# The LID and NMP domains move around the stable CORE as the enzyme transitions between the opened and closed conformations. One way to quantify this movement is by calculating the root mean square deviation (RMSD) of atomic positions.\n\nu = mda.Universe(PSF, DCD)  # closed AdK (PDB ID: 1AKE)\nref = mda.Universe(PSF, CRD)  # open AdK (PDB ID: 4AKE)\n\n# ## Background\n#\n# The root mean square deviation (RMSD) of particle coordinates is one measure of distance, or dissimilarity, between molecular conformations. Each structure should have matching elementwise atoms $i$ in the same order, as the distance between them is calculated and summed for the final result. It is calculated between coordinate arrays $\\mathbf{x}$ and $\\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}$ according to the equation below:\n#\n# $$ \\text{RMSD}(\\mathbf{x}, \\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}) = \\sqrt{\\frac{1}{n} \\sum_{i=1}^{n}{|\\mathbf{x}_i-\\mathbf{x}_i^{\\text{ref}}|^2}} $$\n#\n# As molecules can move around, the structure $\\mathbf{x}$ is usually translated by a vector $\\mathbf{t}$ and rotated by a matrix $\\mathsf{R}$ to align with the reference $\\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}$ such that the RMSD is minimised. The RMSD after this optimal superposition can be expressed as follows:\n#\n# $$ \\text{RMSD}(\\mathbf{x}, \\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}) = \\min_{\\mathsf{R}, \\mathbf{t}} %\n#   \\sqrt{\\frac{1}{N} \\sum_{i=1}^{N} \\left[ %\n#       (\\mathsf{R}\\cdot\\mathbf{x}_{i}(t) + \\mathbf{t}) - \\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\\text{ref}} \\right]^{2}}$$\n#\n# The RMSD between one reference state and a trajectory of structures is often calculated as a way to measure the dissimilarity of the trajectory conformational ensemble to the reference. This reference is frequently the first frame of the trajectory (the default in MDAnalysis), in which case it can provide insight into the overall movement from the initial starting point. While stable RMSD values from a reference structure are frequently used as a measure of conformational convergence, this metric suffers from the problem of *degeneracy*: many different structures can have the same RMSD from the same reference. For an alternative measure, you could use [pairwise or 2D RMSD](pairwise_rmsd.ipynb).\n#\n# Typically not all coordinates in a structures are included in an RMSD analysis. With proteins, the fluctuation of the residue side-chains is not representative of overall conformational change. Therefore when RMSD analyses are performed to investigate large-scale movements in proteins, the atoms are usually restricted only to the backbone atoms (forming the amide-bond chain) or the alpha-carbon atoms. \n#\n# MDAnalysis provides functions and classes to calculate the [RMSD between coordinate arrays](#RMSD-between-two-sets-of-coordinates), and [Universes](#RMSD-of-a-Universe-with-multiple-selections) or [AtomGroups](#RMSD-of-an-AtomGroup-with-multiple-selections). \n#\n# The contribution of each particle $i$ to the final RMSD value can also [be weighted](#Weighted-RMSD-of-a-trajectory) by $w_i$:\n#\n# $$ \\text{RMSD}(\\mathbf{x}, \\mathbf{x}^\\text{ref}) = \\sqrt{\\frac{\\sum_{i=1}^{n}{w_i|\\mathbf{x}_i-\\mathbf{x}_i^{\\text{ref}}|^2}}{\\sum_{i-1}^n w_i}} $$\n#\n# RMSD analyses are frequently weighted by mass. The MDAnalysis RMSD class ([API docs](https://docs.mdanalysis.org/stable/documentation_pages/analysis/rms.html#MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.RMSD)) allows you to both [select mass-weighting](#Mass) with `weights='mass'` or `weights_groupselections='mass'`, or to [pass custom arrays](#Custom-weights) into either keyword.\n\n# ## RMSD between two sets of coordinates\n\n# The ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.rmsd`` function returns the root mean square deviation (in Angstrom) between two sets of coordinates. Here, we calculate the RMSD between the backbone atoms of the open and closed conformations of AdK. Only considering the backbone atoms is often more helpful than calculating the RMSD for all the atoms, as movement in amino acid side-chains isn't indicative of overall conformational change.\n\nrms.rmsd(u.select_atoms('backbone').positions,  # coordinates to align\n         ref.select_atoms('backbone').positions,  # reference coordinates\n         center=True,  # subtract the center of geometry\n         superposition=True)  # superimpose coordinates\n\n# ## RMSD of a Universe with multiple selections\n\n# It is more efficient to use the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.RMSD`` class to calculate the RMSD of an entire trajectory to a single reference point, than to use the the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.rmsd`` function.\n#\n# The ``rms.RMSD`` class first performs a rotational and translational alignment of the target trajectory to the reference universe at ``ref_frame``, using the atoms in ``select`` to determine the transformation. The RMSD of the ``select`` selection is calculated. Then, *without further alignment*, the RMSD of each group in ``groupselections`` is calculated. \n\nCORE = 'backbone and (resid 1-29 or resid 60-121 or resid 160-214)'\nLID = 'backbone and resid 122-159'\nNMP = 'backbone and resid 30-59'\n\nR = rms.RMSD(u,  # universe to align\n             u,  # reference universe or atomgroup\n             select='backbone',  # group to superimpose and calculate RMSD\n             groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP],  # groups for RMSD\n             ref_frame=0)  # frame index of the reference\nR.run()\n\n# The data is saved in ``R.rmsd`` as an array.\n\nR.results.rmsd.shape\n\n# ``R.rmsd`` has a row for each timestep. The first two columns of each row are the frame index of the time step, and the time (which is guessed in trajectory formats without timesteps). The third column is RMSD of ``select``. The last few columns are the RMSD of the groups in ``groupselections``.\n\n# ### Plotting the data\n#\n# We can easily plot this data using the common data analysis package [pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org). We turn the ``R.rmsd`` array into a [DataFrame](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/dsintro.html#dataframe) and label each column below.\n\ndf = pd.DataFrame(R.results.rmsd, \n                  columns=['Frame', 'Time (ns)', \n                           'Backbone', 'CORE', \n                           'LID', 'NMP'])\n\ndf\n\nax = df.plot(x='Frame', y=['Backbone', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'],\n             kind='line')\nax.set_ylabel(r'RMSD ($\\AA$)')\n\n# ## RMSD of an AtomGroup with multiple selections\n#\n# The `RMSD` class accepts both `AtomGroup`s and `Universe`s as arguments. Restricting the atoms considered to an AtomGroup can be very helpful, as the `select` and `groupselections` arguments are applied only to the atoms in the original `AtomGroup`. In the example below, for example, only the alpha-carbons of the CORE domain are incorporated in the analysis.\n#\n# <div class=\"alert alert-info\">\n#     \n# **Note**\n#\n# This feature does not currently support `groupselections`.\n#\n# </div>\n\nca = u.select_atoms('name CA')\n\nR = rms.RMSD(ca, ca, select=CORE, ref_frame=0)\nR.run()\n\ndf = pd.DataFrame(R.results.rmsd, \n                  columns=['Frame', 'Time (ns)', \n                           'CORE'])\n\nax = df.plot(x='Frame', y='CORE', kind='line')\nax.set_ylabel('RMSD ($\\AA$)')\n\n# ## Weighted RMSD of a trajectory\n#\n# You can also calculate the weighted RMSD of a trajectory using the `weights` and `weights_groupselections` keywords. The former only applies weights to the group in `select`, while the latter must be a list of the *same length and order* as `groupselections`. If you would like to only weight certain groups in `groupselections`, use `None` for the unweighted groups. Both `weights` and `weights_groupselections` accept `None` (for unweighted), `'mass'` (to weight by mass), and custom arrays. A custom array should have the same number of values as there are particles in the corresponding AtomGroup.\n\n# ### Mass\n\n# It is common to weight RMSD analyses by particle weight, so the `RMSD` class accepts `'mass'` as an argument for `weights`. Note that the `weights` keyword only applies to the group in `select`, and does not apply to the `groupselections`; these remain unweighted below.\n\nR_mass = rms.RMSD(u, u,\n                  select='protein and name CA',\n                  weights='mass',\n                  groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP])\nR_mass.run()\n\n# The plot looks largely the same as above because all the alpha-carbons and individual backbone atoms have the same mass. Below we show how you can pass in custom weights.\n\ndf_mass = pd.DataFrame(R_mass.results.rmsd, \n                       columns=['Frame', \n                                'Time (ns)', \n                                'C-alphas', 'CORE', \n                                'LID', 'NMP'])\nax_mass = df_mass.plot(x='Frame', \n                       y=['C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'])\nax_mass.set_ylabel('Mass-weighted RMSD ($\\AA$)')\n\n# ### Custom weights\n\n# You can also pass in an array of values for the weights. This must have the same length as the number of atoms in your selection groups. In this example, we pass in arrays of residue numbers. This **is not a typical weighting you might choose**, but we use it here to show how you can get different results to the previous graphs for mass-weighted and non-weighted RMSD. You could choose to pass in an array of charges, or your own custom value. \n#\n# First we select the atom groups to make this easier.\n\nag = u.select_atoms('protein and name CA')\nprint('Shape of C-alpha charges:', ag.charges.shape)\ncore = u.select_atoms(CORE)\nlid = u.select_atoms(LID)\nnmp = u.select_atoms(NMP)\n\n# Below, we pass in weights for `ag` with the `weights` keyword, and weights for the `groupselections` with the `weights_groupselections` keyword.\n\nR_charge = rms.RMSD(u, u,\n                    select='protein and name CA',\n                    groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP],\n                    weights=ag.resids,\n                    weights_groupselections=[core.resids, \n                                             lid.resids, \n                                             nmp.resids])\nR_charge.run()\n\n# You can see in the below graph that the NMP domain has much higher RMSD than before, as each particle is weighted by its residue number. Conversely, the CORE domain doesn't really change much. We could potentially infer from this that residues later in the NMP domain (with a higher residue number) are mobile during the length of the trajectory, whereas residues later in the CORE domain do not seem to contribute significantly to the RMSD.\n#\n# However, again, this is a **very non-conventional metric** and is shown here simply to demonstrate how to use the code.\n\ndf_charge = pd.DataFrame(R_charge.results.rmsd, \n                         columns=['Frame', \n                                'Time (ns)', \n                                'C-alphas', 'CORE', \n                                'LID', 'NMP'])\nax_charge = df_charge.plot(x='Frame',\n                           y=['C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'])\nax_charge.set_ylabel('Charge-weighted RMSD ($\\AA$)')\n\n# ## References\n#\n# [1] Oliver Beckstein, Elizabeth&nbsp;J.     "task_brief": "# Task: RMSD analysis of the adenylate kinase open\u2194closed transition\n\nAdenylate kinase (AdK) has a stable CORE domain flanked by the LID and NMP domains, which move as the enzyme transitions between closed and open conformations. You are supplied with the topology, a trajectory sampling the closed\u2192open transition, and the open-conformation coordinates. Quantify this conformational change by computing the root mean square deviation (RMSD) of atomic positions, in Angstrom, in five analyses below.\n\n## Supplied inputs\n\n- `inputs/adk.psf` \u2014 protein topology (PSF) for the AdK structure; 214 residues with atom counts and atom order shared by all supplied coordinate data.\n- `inputs/adk_trajectory.dcd` \u2014 trajectory (DCD) sampling the closed\u2192open transition.\n- `inputs/adk_open.crd` \u2014 coordinates (CRD) of the open conformation of the same structure.\n\n(File byte identities are pinned separately at task setup.)\n\n## Definitions\n\nFor coordinate arrays **x** (one row per atom, atoms in matching order between compared structures) and reference **x**^(ref):\n\n- **RMSD(x, x^(ref)) = sqrt( (1/n) \u03a3\u1d62 |x\u1d62 \u2212 x\u1d62^(ref)|\u00b2 )**\n- **Weighted RMSD(x, x^(ref)) = sqrt( \u03a3\u1d62 w\u1d62 |x\u1d62 \u2212 x\u1d62^(ref)|\u00b2 / \u03a3\u1d62 w\u1d62 )** (invariant to any overall positive scaling of the weights).\n- **Optimal superposition**: the displacement / rotation pair that minimizes the (weighted) RMSD; rotations are proper (determinant +1). RMSD under optimal superposition is the minimum over such pairs, with coordinates first expressed relative to the appropriate weighted centroid.\n- **Backbone atoms**: the main-chain protein atoms (N, CA, C, O).\n- **Domains** (residue numbers as in the topology):\n  - CORE = backbone atoms of residues 1\u201329, 60\u2013121, 160\u2013214\n  - LID = backbone atoms of residues 122\u2013159\n  - NMP = backbone atoms of residues 30\u201359\n\n## Required analyses\n\n**A. Open vs. closed endpoint conformations.** RMSD between the backbone atoms of the open structure (`adk_open.crd`) and the trajectory's first frame (closed conformation). Subtract the center of geometry of each set, apply optimal superposition, and report the resulting backbone RMSD.\n\n**B\u2013E. Trajectory RMSD versus frame 0.** For each of the analyses below, the reference is frame 0 of the trajectory itself. For each trajectory frame, first superimpose the frame onto frame 0 by the optimal (weighted, where weights are specified) rigid-body transformation determined by the fitting group; then report:\n\n1. the RMSD of the fitting group under that fit; and\n2. for each listed domain group, the RMSD between the frame's transformed coordinates and the **untransformed frame-0 coordinates** of that group's atoms, **computed without any further fitting, centering, or re-alignment** of the group (the group RMSD measures residual domain displacement under the single global superposition).\n\n**B. Backbone and domains (unweighted).** Fitting group: all backbone atoms, unweighted. Report four series: backbone (under the fit), CORE, LID, NMP (group RMSDs, unweighted). Group atom sets are the backbone atoms of the full structure given by the domain definitions above.\n\n**C. CORE restricted to alpha-carbons.** Restrict the entire analysis to the alpha-carbon (CA) atoms. Fitting group: the alpha-carbons of the CORE domain. Report the CORE fit RMSD.\n\n**D. Mass-weighted.** Fitting group: all alpha-carbons of the protein, with each atom weighted by its mass (mass-weighted centroids for the superposition). Report the mass-weighted fit RMSD for the alpha-carbons, and mass-weighted group RMSDs for CORE, LID, NMP. Group atom sets are the backbone atoms of the **full structure** (not restricted to alpha-carbons), and the group RMSDs are also mass-weighted (each atom weighted by its mass).\n\n**E. Residue-number-weighted.** Same structure as D, but each atom is weighted by its residue number instead of its mass \u2014 in the fitting group (alpha-carbons of the protein) and in the CORE, LID, NMP group RMSDs (backbone atoms, full structure, weighted by residue number).\n\nNote that in D and E the fitting group and the reported group RMSDs use the specified weighting; the groups being compared are the full-structure backbone atom sets, independent of the alpha-carbon restriction on the fitting group.\n\n## Required outputs\n\nWrite CSV files (UTF-8, one header row, comma-separated). All RMSD values are in Angstrom and must be finite. Each trajectory table contains exactly one row per trajectory frame, ordered by strictly increasing frame index (the row order is the time series). The frame column is the 0-based trajectory frame index. Do not output a time column.\n\n1. `outputs/rmsd_backbone_open_closed.csv` \u2014 analysis A. Columns: `rmsd_backbone_angstrom`. One data row.\n2. `outputs/rmsd_backbone_domains.csv` \u2014 analysis B. Columns: `frame`, `rmsd_backbone_angstrom`, `rmsd_core_angstrom`, `rmsd_lid_angstrom`, `rmsd_nmp_angstrom`.\n3. `outputs/rmsd_ca_core.csv` \u2014 analysis C. Columns: `frame`, `rmsd_core_ca_angstrom`.\n4. `outputs/rmsd_mass_weighted.csv` \u2014 analysis D. Columns: `frame`, `rmsd_ca_mass_angstrom`, `rmsd_core_mass_angstrom`, `rmsd_lid_mass_angstrom`, `rmsd_nmp_mass_angstrom`.\n5. `outputs/rmsd_residue_weighted.csv` \u2014 analysis E. Columns: `frame`, `rmsd_ca_resid_angstrom`, `rmsd_core_resid_angstrom`, `rmsd_lid_resid_angstrom`, `rmsd_nmp_resid_angstrom`.\n\nThe frame identity is shared across outputs 2\u20135: each must cover exactly the same set of trajectory frames, once each, in the same order. The RMSD at frame 0 is expected to be near zero (floating-point rounding of identical conformations), not exactly zero.\n\n## Environment and limits\n\nCPU-only; no network access; run within 600 seconds and 8 GiB RAM. Software choice is open: any tools may be used as long as the outputs above are produced. For convenience, a compatible offline environment (MDAnalysis 2.11.0, NumPy, pandas) can be supplied; using it is not a requirement. If you use MDAnalysis, note that its `RMSD` class's current semantics for `weights='mass'` (mass applied to group selections as well) match the definitions in D above."

  "instruction": "# Task: RMSD analysis of the adenylate kinase open\u2194closed transition\n\nAdenylate kinase (AdK) has a stable CORE domain flanked by the LID and NMP domains, which move as the enzyme transitions between closed and open conformations. You are supplied with the topology, a trajectory sampling the closed\u2192open transition, and the open-conformation coordinates. Quantify this conformational change by computing the root mean square deviation (RMSD) of atomic positions, in Angstrom, in five analyses below.\n\n## Supplied inputs\n\n- `inputs/adk.psf` \u2014 protein topology (PSF) for the AdK structure; 214 residues with atom counts and atom order shared by all supplied coordinate data.\n- `inputs/adk_trajectory.dcd` \u2014 trajectory (DCD) sampling the closed\u2192open transition.\n- `inputs/adk_open.crd` \u2014 coordinates (CRD) of the open conformation of the same structure.\n\n## Definitions\n\nFor coordinate arrays **x** (one row per atom, atoms in matching order between compared structures) and reference **x**^(ref):\n\n- **RMSD(x, x^(ref)) = sqrt( (1/n) \u03a3\u1d62 |x\u1d62 \u2212 x\u1d62^(ref)|\u00b2 )**\n- **Weighted RMSD(x, x^(ref)) = sqrt( \u03a3\u1d62 w\u1d62 |x\u1d62 \u2212 x\u1d62^(ref)|\u00b2 / \u03a3\u1d62 w\u1d62 )** (invariant to any overall positive scaling of the weights).\n- **Optimal superposition**: the displacement / rotation pair that minimizes the (weighted) RMSD; rotations are proper (determinant +1). RMSD under optimal superposition is the minimum over such pairs, with coordinates first expressed relative to the appropriate weighted centroid.\n- **Backbone atoms**: the main-chain protein atoms (N, CA, C, O).\n- **Domains** (residue numbers as in the topology):\n  - CORE = backbone atoms of residues 1\u201329, 60\u2013121, 160\u2013214\n  - LID = backbone atoms of residues 122\u2013159\n  - NMP = backbone atoms of residues 30\u201359\n\n## Required analyses\n\n**A. Open vs. closed endpoint conformations.** RMSD between the backbone atoms of the open structure (`adk_open.crd`) and the trajectory's first frame (closed conformation). Subtract the center of geometry of each set, apply optimal superposition, and report the resulting backbone RMSD.\n\n**B\u2013E. Trajectory RMSD versus frame 0.** For each of the analyses below, the reference is frame 0 of the trajectory itself. For each trajectory frame, first superimpose the frame onto frame 0 by the optimal (weighted, where weights are specified) rigid-body transformation determined by the fitting group; then report:\n\n1. the RMSD of the fitting group under that fit; and\n2. for each listed domain group, the RMSD between the frame's transformed coordinates and the **untransformed frame-0 coordinates** of that group's atoms, **computed without any further fitting, centering, or re-alignment** of the group (the group RMSD measures residual domain displacement under the single global superposition).\n\n**B. Backbone and domains (unweighted).** Fitting group: all backbone atoms, unweighted. Report four series: backbone (under the fit), CORE, LID, NMP (group RMSDs, unweighted). Group atom sets are the backbone atoms of the full structure given by the domain definitions above.\n\n**C. CORE restricted to alpha-carbons.** Restrict the entire analysis to the alpha-carbon (CA) atoms. Fitting group: the alpha-carbons of the CORE domain. Report the CORE fit RMSD.\n\n**D. Mass-weighted.** Fitting group: all alpha-carbons of the protein, with each atom weighted by its mass (mass-weighted centroids for the superposition). Report the mass-weighted fit RMSD for the alpha-carbons, and mass-weighted group RMSDs for CORE, LID, NMP. Group atom sets are the backbone atoms of the **full structure** (not restricted to alpha-carbons), and the group RMSDs are also mass-weighted (each atom weighted by its mass).\n\n**E. Residue-number-weighted.** Same structure as D, but each atom is weighted by its residue number instead of its mass \u2014 in the fitting group (alpha-carbons of the protein) and in the CORE, LID, NMP group RMSDs (backbone atoms, full structure, weighted by residue number).\n\nNote that in D and E the fitting group and the reported group RMSDs use the specified weighting; the groups being compared are the full-structure backbone atom sets, independent of the alpha-carbon restriction on the fitting group.\n\n## Required outputs\n\nWrite CSV files (UTF-8, one header row, comma-separated) under `outputs/`. All RMSD values are in Angstrom and must be finite. Each trajectory table contains exactly one row per trajectory frame, ordered by strictly increasing frame index (the row order is the time series). The frame column is the 0-based trajectory frame index. Do not output a time column.\n\n1. `outputs/rmsd_backbone_open_closed.csv` \u2014 analysis A. Columns: `rmsd_backbone_angstrom`. One data row.\n2. `outputs/rmsd_backbone_domains.csv` \u2014 analysis B. Columns: `frame`, `rmsd_backbone_angstrom`, `rmsd_core_angstrom`, `rmsd_lid_angstrom`, `rmsd_nmp_angstrom`.\n3. `outputs/rmsd_ca_core.csv` \u2014 analysis C. Columns: `frame`, `rmsd_core_ca_angstrom`.\n4. `outputs/rmsd_mass_weighted.csv` \u2014 analysis D. Columns: `frame`, `rmsd_ca_mass_angstrom`, `rmsd_core_mass_angstrom`, `rmsd_lid_mass_angstrom`, `rmsd_nmp_mass_angstrom`.\n5. `outputs/rmsd_resid_weighted.csv` \u2014 analysis E. Columns: `frame`, `rmsd_ca_resid_angstrom`, `rmsd_core_resid_angstrom`, `rmsd_lid_resid_angstrom`, `rmsd_nmp_resid_angstrom`.\n\nThe frame identity is shared across outputs 2\u20135: each must cover exactly the same set of trajectory frames, once each, in the same order. The RMSD at frame 0 is expected to be near zero (floating-point rounding of identical conformations), not exactly zero.\n\n## Environment and limits\n\nCPU-only; no network access; run within 600 seconds and 8 GiB RAM.
